A cutting-edge method is introduced for image reconstruction using compressed sensing data, which leverages the inherent group structure in images through multi-level grouping and employs a non-convex sparsity-promoting function to effectively capture image sparsity. By combining these approaches, the method can effectively handle images with heavy noise and artifacts, and is capable of producing high-quality reconstruction results. Experimental results demonstrate that the method significantly outperforms traditional image reconstruction techniques, yielding superior results in terms of visual quality and numerical assessment.

In the field of computer vision, the task of recognizing facial skin disease is particularly demanding. To address this, researchers have developed an innovative approach called RethNet, which employs an object-by-object learning method to identify and localize facial skin disease. RethNet leverages a multi-stage technique to break down the complex process into three distinct phases: initial segmentation, problem localization, and final classification. Initially, the network segments the face, followed by the identification and segmentation of skin problems using a refined attention mechanism, and finally, the network classifies each skin issue. RethNet demonstrates significant improvements over existing methods, with remarkable accuracy rates of 94.1% and 96.7% for recognition and localization tasks, respectively.

In the context of consecutive decoding of low-density parity-check codes, we examine the properties of short chain codes and present analytical methods to calculate the probability distribution of the number of errors corrected during consecutive decoding. This is achieved by deriving the probability distribution of the syndrome and using it to calculate the probability distribution of the number of errors corrected. We also demonstrate that the expected value of syndrome bits through consecutive decoding remains constant and is directly related to the length of the decoder. This allows us to simplify our analysis of analytical methods. Numerical simulations are presented to validate the proposed analytical methods, and our findings reveal that the proposed methods can accurately predict the performance of PAC codes under consecutive decoding.

Online recommender systems have become increasingly reliant on user suggestions to enhance interaction and engagement. However, a significant concern arises for systems with "cold-start" users who have no prior history, resulting in poor recommendation quality. To address this issue, researchers have developed sequential suggestion systems that aim to establish a connection with these users through iterative recommendations. By doing so, the system can refine its understanding of the user's preferences while minimizing the risk of making errors. To achieve this balance, a new approach called MetaTL has been proposed, which incorporates transitional learning. MetaTL uses a pre-trained meta-learning model to adapt to the user's preferences, allowing it to make more accurate recommendations over time. By incorporating a transition module, the system can refine its performance on complex tasks, such as ranking items across multiple categories. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of MetaTL, showcasing its ability to achieve superior results compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

Recent observations of Ultra High Energy Galactic cosmic rays are compelling new evidence that radio galaxies are the primary sources of UHECRs in the universe, with certain radiopulsars potentially serving as accelerators of UHECRs. This perspective is reinforced by data from the Pierre Auger Observatory and the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, as well as by theoretical models of UHECR generation and the cosmic ray halo. These findings are further supported by the analysis of UHECR events recorded by both observatories, which reveals a significant correlation between radiopulsars and UHECR events in the data from the Pierre Auger Observatory.

The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft's collision with Dimorphos will transfer momentum to alter its orbital velocity, but the specific method of momentum transfer varies depending on whether the collision is with a spherical object or one with a defined elliptical shape. To analyze this, researchers simulated the gravitational influence of the target's extended area on a spherical projectile with the aid of a computational code. Their study revealed significant differences in momentum transfer for an elliptical object in comparison to a spherical one, with the former experiencing increased gravitational pull near its focal points. To accurately model the DART mission's momentum transfer, researchers must consider the target's elongated shape, as the gravitational influence of the target's extended area is not sufficient to account for the discrepancy in momentum.

This study introduces a neural network architecture for fusing High Dynamic Range (HDR) images into a single Intensity Image (II) that can be used for through-the-windshield driver recognition. We propose a simple, unrolled neural network called the Mertens Unrolled Network (MUN) that incorporates the Mertens fusion algorithm and allows for end-to-end learning of both image fusion and classification. We also present a more advanced version of this network, referred to as the Mertens Unrolled with Attention Network (MUNAN), which incorporates a multi-scale attention module to focus on the most relevant regions of the input images. By using both fully convolutional and attention-based models, we are able to achieve high accuracy while reducing the number of parameters. We have tested our network on the public ImageNet-HDR dataset and achieved a high accuracy of 90.2% on the test set, while also outperforming other state-of-the-art methods with lower parameter counts.

In 2019, the German research ministry established the National Research Data Infrastructure, which prioritizes long-term data preservation. Although this is a crucial aspect, particularly in the social and behavioral sciences, where data is often open-source and shared with the public, this prioritization sometimes contradicts the design of open-source data repositories. Our research focuses on the development of an extensive, open-source repository for language-related data, which we have dubbed the Comprehensive Blub Archive Network. Our goal is to identify the key design principles that should guide the creation of open-source data repositories, which we achieve by implementing these guidelines within our own archive. Our work is a direct result of a collaborative, research-based effort that informs our recommendations.

This study develops a novel approach to handling multiple types of missing data in both outcomes and covariates, which we categorize into three types: unobservable in nature; partially observable but with hidden components; and completely unobservable. We establish a framework for estimating regression models that account for these data types and introduce a new class of estimators, which we call multistage estimators. We demonstrate that these multistage estimators outperform existing methods, particularly when dealing with a large number of unobserved covariates, as evident in their asymptotic performance and finite-sample results. Furthermore, we introduce a multistage estimator for incomplete outcome variables and evaluate its performance through simulation studies and real-world applications, such as in the analysis of incomplete survey data and medical claims information.

A widely recognized series expansion of the complete elliptic integral of the first kind, using the inverse hyperbolic tangent, has been extensively utilized in various fields of applied mathematics. This note aims to resolve a longstanding conjecture regarding the accuracy of the series expansion by providing a definitive formula, thereby facilitating the practical implementation of series expansions for elliptic integrals.

This paper introduces Decomposed Inductive Process Learning, a novel approach that utilizes a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework to efficiently acquire optimal policies in complex, large-scale Markov decision processes. By breaking down the learning process into manageable sub-problems, our method enables the agents to focus on the most critical states, thereby significantly reducing the sample requirements needed to achieve near-optimal performance. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach through extensive experiments on multiple benchmark environments, and our results show that DIL outperforms previous methods by achieving near-optimal performance with substantially reduced sample requirements.

The widespread dissemination of fabricated information through the internet has given rise to a new form of misinformation known as "fake news." In this study, a novel approach to generating English and Arabic fabricated news articles is presented, along with the development of a dataset consisting of fabricated and genuine news articles. This dataset is utilized to investigate the effectiveness of advanced artificial intelligence methods in distinguishing fabricated from genuine news articles. To this end, three artificial intelligence models are developed and their performance is evaluated on the fabricated and genuine news articles dataset. Our experiments reveal that the use of artificial intelligence in detecting fake news in Arabic language media is still in its infancy and requires further research.

A correction to a previous publication is presented. The original paper "Torsion subgroups of elliptic curves defined over all D4 extensions of the rational numbers" initially incorrectly identified the D4 extensions as certain quadratic fields, specifically K = Q(√2) and K = Q(√-1). The correct interpretation should be that Q(√2) corresponds to D4, whereas Q(√-1) corresponds to D4'.

In complex multiqubit quantum systems with entanglement that extends beyond individual pairs, the relationships between different qubits are not limited to their immediate counterparts. We have developed a computational method that employs matrix product operators to investigate and characterize these nonlocal connections. This method enables us to model and simulate various quantum systems, including those undergoing quench dynamics or subjected to periodic driving, the dynamics of spin chains with long-range interactions, and the effects of noise on individual qubits or the environment. We have demonstrated that a specific type of noise can induce the formation of nonlocal entanglement in spin chains with long-range interactions. This discovery has significant implications for our understanding of complex quantum systems, particularly in the context of quantum thermodynamics and the behavior of open quantum systems.

In various web domains, such as static web pages and dedicated web applications, the effectiveness of crawling can be significantly improved by reducing the need for crawling the same content multiple times. To address this, we developed a novel machine learning-based crawling method that learns and preserves the site's internal link structure. By simulating a user navigating a site's pages, our method models the site's hierarchy and prioritizes the most informative pages. It also optimizes crawling efficiency by limiting the number of fresh pages discovered to the site's most recently visited pages. By incorporating user interaction signals, our method can further enhance its performance. Notably, it outperforms existing targeted crawling approaches in both simulated and real-world experiments, achieving a 2-3x improvement.

A system known as object-centric event networks (OCENs) is used to track and analyze complex data from various sources such as social media, healthcare records, and more. OCENs are represented through a directed graph consisting of objects linked by events, making it a versatile tool for numerous applications. One of the key challenges in OCENs lies in developing a framework to identify patterns within the data, particularly in instances where the connections between events are not predetermined or consistently applied. In an effort to address this challenge, we propose a method for defining patterns within OCENs based on the relationships between different object and event types. By utilizing these definitions, we are able to extract a subgraph from the OCEN that corresponds to the specified pattern. Furthermore, we introduce a method for automatically discovering these pattern definitions within OCENs. By leveraging these definitions, we are able to identify the presence of known patterns within the OCEN and even discover new ones through the use of a clustering algorithm. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through the analysis of two distinct datasets, one originating from healthcare and the other from social media, with varying levels of noise and uncertainty.

A novel method for restoring wavefields is proposed, which incorporates limited-subspace weighted matrix factorizations. By factorizing the covariance matrix of the gradient of the forward-modelled data into three orthogonal components, and utilizing a maximum a posteriori estimate with a Gaussian prior, the method addresses the ill-posedness of the inverse problem and regularizes the solution. Unlike traditional regularizers, the geometric structure of the gradient allows the regularizing effect to be tied to the physical properties of the inverse problem. Specifically, the method's regularizers are related to the spatial coherence of the reflector orientation, making it a geophysically informed regularization. To improve the method's efficiency, a computationally inexpensive implementation of the regularizers is introduced. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical experiments on synthetic data.

Metalenses have the potential to replace traditional optical systems due to their compact design, simplicity, and cost-effectiveness compared to their mechanical counterparts. However, most research has focused on metalenses that focus a single wavelength, whereas real-world applications require lenses that can focus a broad spectrum of wavelengths in focus. Our research presents a metalens that uses a quadratic phase design to focus a wide range of wavelengths in focus, making it suitable for use in various applications such as image processing, spectroscopy, and light detection. Our findings show that metalenses with a specific design of curved phase plates can focus different wavelengths at the same point, making them ideal for use in real-world optical systems.

We have developed a novel approach to plasma-assisted atmospheric pressure therapy, leveraging radio-frequency diffuse plasma jets that operate in neutral environments. A key advantage of these plasma jets is that they produce few radicals, making them suitable for treating living cells. In this study, we present a theoretical model that describes the electrical behavior of RF APPJs with neutral plasmas, focusing on the interaction between plasma and gas phases. Our model shows that the plasma and gas phases evolve over time, eventually reaching a steady state. We also examine the impact of plasma input power, gas flow, and plasma volume on APPJ performance and their effects on plasma and gas phases.

This research examines the influence of string theory corrections on black holes' quasinormal modes and silhouettes in $d$-dimensional spacetimes with a scalar field source. We derive quasinormal frequencies in both general relativity and string theory within the eikonal approximation, revealing that under general relativity, the real and imaginary components of these frequencies increase with angular momentum, whereas under string theory, the real components decrease and imaginary components increase. Furthermore, we investigate how the ratio of real to imaginary frequencies varies according to the angular momentum parameter. Additionally, we investigate how the thickness of a black hole's shadow is impacted by string theory corrections and scalar field properties.

Pulsar Timing Array experiments are designed to identify and study the gravitational wave background by analyzing data from multiple pulsars, offering insights into the universe's early history. Two methods, commonly employed to detect a common gravitational wave signal across multiple pulsars, are the common-spectrum and cross-correlation techniques. We investigate the effectiveness of these methods using simulated data based on the data from three pulsars, and we find that the cross-correlation method outperforms the common-spectrum method in terms of detecting a wide range of gravitational wave frequencies. Our results are supported by analytical calculations and highlight the importance of the correlation coefficient in determining the sensitivity of these methods.

In the context of Construction-A, where a code is supported on a subset of the permutation matrix set, this note derives sufficient and necessary conditions for the generator matrix of the code. By considering the GHW of rows in generator and parity check matrices, lower and upper bounds are established for the GHW of rows in parity check matrices. A condition based on the Hamming distance between code words is also established for the SCD property of the generator matrix.

This research introduces a concept of truncated operators with unbounded symbols, extending a well-known type of operators originally defined by Arvesleben. The study connects these operators to matrix-valued truncated Wiener-Hopf operators with unbounded symbols, establishing a key relationship between the two. Furthermore, it outlines conditions for when extended versions of these operators are equivalent. The research also explores a special case involving matrix-valued truncated Toeplitz operators, establishing a key relationship with a related operator. The study concludes by outlining possible directions for further investigation.

In clinical trials, researchers often examine multiple endpoints and investigate how initial results might affect subsequent findings. A Bayesian approach, specifically posterior proportional influence, quantifies this anticipated impact. The method calculates an estimate's influence on future analyses, allowing researchers to adjust sample size or gather more data if anticipated findings are unsatisfying. A key benefit is the ability to evaluate early results' influence while still treating the trial as an ongoing, not completed, investigation. A recent study applied this method to a clinical trial investigating the treatment of severe COVID-19.

This study introduces an unsupervised method for audio anomaly detection that
operates effectively even when there's a mismatch between the training and test
data sources. It's based on a combination of unsupervised embedding using
dimensionality reduction followed by an anomaly detection step, where the
anomaly score is derived from the reduced data space. We evaluate the approach
using the MAESTRO dataset, which is particularly suitable for anomaly detection
tasks, and compare its performance with that of an unsupervised baseline model
trained on a different dataset. We also explore the impact of using different
dimensionality reduction techniques on the approach's overall accuracy.

In a three-dimensional system consisting of a Fermi gas with a small number of distinct spin states and interacting with other identical particles via a specific $1/r^a$ potential, we investigate the behavior of the system when the number of particles approaches zero. Our research reveals that the ground state energy exhibits a complex pattern as the number of particles changes, featuring both a deep minimum and several local maxima. The emergence of this intricate structure can be attributed to a phenomenon known as fermionic magnetism, where a small region within the system behaves like a magnet, characterized by an energy barrier that hinders the system's motion. Our study demonstrates that the ground state energy's non-trivial behavior is a result of the interplay between the system's magnetic properties and the effects of the vanishing particle count, and this is distinct from a similar phenomenon observed in the study of two-dimensional systems.

The primary goal of our research is to refine the sample of known pulsars emitting gamma-rays and to determine the precise physical characteristics of pulsars, specifically pulsar magnetic fields and distances. We have conducted a study on 116 pulsars, utilizing data from the 2nd Fermi-LAT catalog, and developed a new method to categorize them. We have created a new sample of pulsars, eliminating those with incomplete information, and applied a novel classification technique to distinguish pulsars with low, intermediate, and high spin-down luminosities. We have also employed machine learning to classify pulsars, utilizing features such as spin frequency, age, and magnetic field. We have applied a probabilistic model to determine the distance distribution of each pulsar category, and derived the distance distribution for each category. We have also applied a probabilistic model to determine the distance distribution of each pulsar, and compared it with the distribution obtained from radio surveys. We have also analyzed the distribution of Fermi-LAT pulsars and compared it with the distribution of pulsars with low, intermediate, and high spin-down luminosities. We have also analyzed the distribution of pulsars and found that the distribution of pulsars with low, intermediate, and high spin-down luminosities is consistent with the distribution of pulsars emitting gamma-rays. We have also analyzed the distribution of pulsars and found that the distribution of pulsars with low, intermediate, and high spin-down luminosities is consistent with the distribution

The quantum Hall effect is characterized by a series of quantized energy levels at integer and fractional charges, resulting from the interplay between electrons and magnetic fields. The fractional quantum Hall effect is notable for its unique fractional charge at the nodal points of fractional Landau levels. The energy levels of these fractional Landau levels exhibit distinct patterns, with a gap separating the highest from the lowest states. The presence of these gaps has been found to influence the energy levels of the surrounding Landau levels, with a unique spectral rule governing the arrangement of energy levels in fractional quantum Hall systems. This spectral rule is a result of the interplay between the energy levels of the fractional Landau levels and the energy levels of the surrounding Landau levels, with a unique total rule governing the energy levels of the system. The energy levels of the system exhibit distinct patterns, with a unique total rule governing the energy levels of the highest and lowest states. The energy levels of the system exhibit distinct patterns, with a unique spectral total rule governing the energy levels of the system.

The network of multi-disciplinary ground-based observatories, referred to as EXTreme Energy Events (EEEs), plays a vital role in investigating high-energy phenomena originating from celestial sources. Comprising 17 locations in Russia, the EEE network features an innovative, wide-field telescope design, known as the OFR-1710, that utilizes optical-fiber reflectors. Each OFR-1710 telescope comprises 1,710 optical fibers, each with a light detector at its end. This unique telescope design, with its 1.8-meter effective aperture, enables the detection of gamma-rays with energies above 10 TeV. This paper provides a detailed examination of the OFR-1710 telescope system, including its optical design, light detection technology, data acquisition process, and data processing algorithms. Additionally, it discusses the various methods employed to enhance the gamma-ray detection efficiency of individual telescopes and the network as a whole.

The Cauchy problem for the truncated Boltzmann equation is investigated with focus on its stability and asymptotic properties when the initial data are minute. It has been found that the solution exhibits exponential propagation of singularities in space-time and a linearized initial boundary value problem for the Boltzmann equation under the condition $0\le g\le 1$.

This research evaluates the reliability of various classifiers in the presence of label noise. A diverse range of classifiers was examined, including both traditional methods such as decision trees and support vector machines, and more advanced techniques like neural networks and gradient boosting. To assess their performance, the classifiers were tested on datasets with clean labels, using which they were initially trained and then left to learn on its own with noisy labels. Comparative metrics, including accuracy, false positives, false negatives, and class F1 scores, were used to gauge the effectiveness of each classifier. Notably, the study found that a probabilistic neural network outperformed other classifiers in terms of accuracy, class F1 scores, and false negatives, followed closely by support vector machine with RBF kernel.

A novel approach to categorizing and analyzing orbit codes is presented by examining automorphism groups and their symmetries. This involves identifying the automorphism group's cyclic structure, determining the cyclic structure of the automorphism group, and classifying the orbit under the automorphism group's action. The paper demonstrates that orbit codes can be uniquely defined by their cyclic structure in the automorphism group, mirroring the characterization of cyclic codes. Similarly, orbit codes can be specified by the cyclotomic invariants of the automorphism group, analogous to cyclic codes. To investigate automorphism group symmetries, the concept of automorphism invariant subgroups is introduced and orbit codes are classified based on these subgroups. A comprehensive framework for categorizing orbit codes is provided, encompassing the main types of orbit codes.

A precise mass measurement of a star near the end of its main sequence in the M67 open cluster has been achieved by combining spectroscopic and photometric data. This was made possible through high-resolution radial velocity measurements of 57 stars near the turnoff, which were then compared to the velocities of 211 brighter, photometrically measured stars. The resulting velocity differences allowed for the calculation of the turnoff stars' mass, which was then confirmed through isochrone fitting of the main sequence stars. The resulting values were 1.61 plus/minus 0.10 solar masses for the turnoff stars. This measurement was then used to determine the age of the cluster, which was found to be approximately 3.365 billion years. This measurement was found to be consistent with previous measurements, and the high precision was attributed to the use of radial velocity measurements to determine the turnoff stars' mass, as opposed to the use of other methods. The resulting values were also found to be in agreement with the expected rate of mass loss during red giant branch evolution, as predicted by theoretical models.

The given paper proves the completeness theorem for an orthonormal set of eigenfunctions associated with the complex Schrödinger operator $\mathscr{L}_c = -\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} + cx^\alpha + \frac{i}{h} \frac{\partial}{\partial x}$, where $h$ is Planck's constant, $c$ is a real constant, and $\alpha$ is a non-negative real number. Specifically, it is shown that an orthonormal set of eigenfunctions $e^{ik}$ for $k\in\mathbb{R}$ provides a complete decomposition of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^+)$ as a closed subspace under the inner product defined by $\langle f, g\rangle = \int_0^\infty f(x)\overline{g(x)}dx$ for functions $f, g \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^+)$.

A recently proposed SPH (smoothed particle hydrodynamics) method has made significant advancements in conserving mass, momentum, and energy, and in handling particle clustering. This new algorithm leverages a weighted averaging technique to mitigate particle clustering, and it achieves higher accuracy in the estimation of spatial and temporal derivatives by employing a second-order polynomial smoothing function. The proposed method demonstrates its potential by applying the SPH framework to various problems, including Sod and Noh problems, and it outperforms existing methods in these test cases. Furthermore, the method shows comparable results when applied to the Noh problem using a third-order smoothing function.

Recent advancements in hyperspectral imaging have led to the development of innovative applications across remote sensing and tracking, however, high-resolution acquisitions are often hindered by lengthy processing times and budget constraints. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel end-to-end deep learning network capable of reconstructing high-quality hyperspectral images from spectral-intensity images efficiently. This network combines two key components: a pixel-aware deep function-blend network that accurately predicts spectral intensities at the pixel level, and a high-resolution spectral image module that generates a high-resolution spectral image from the pixel intensity predictions. Through comprehensive testing on various datasets, our proposed method has achieved state-of-the-art results in spectral super-resolution.

Item geotagging is a crucial task in many applications, but current methods often struggle to handle situations where items are placed in non-human associated geographic locations. To overcome this limitation, we've developed an innovative geotagging approach that leverages the surrounding environment to determine a geotag. By combining a deep neural network and a probabilistic model, our method is able to infer geotags from contextual information and item categories, while also incorporating a geotag validation process to ensure accuracy. The evaluation of our approach on a real-world dataset demonstrates its superior performance compared to existing methods.

The issue of dam reservoir retrieval from satellite imagery is addressed in this study, focusing on developing an image analysis pipeline that can be utilized for dam monitoring. Our method is composed of two key components: a dam detection algorithm and a dam reservoir segmentation model, both of which are supported by tailored loss functions. We tested our approach on a unique dataset of 40 satellite images from diverse sources, which contained a total of 2,576 annotated points and 1,142 instances of dam reservoir information. These inputs were utilized to train two neural networks: the first network identifies dams and returns a point with the highest score, while the second network segments the reservoir associated with the detected dam. Our method was compared with two established techniques, demonstrating superior performance.

This paper introduces F-region ionospheric electron flux into the study of the quarter-frequency solar flux or QFS-region, which is related to the 25 cm wavelength radio signal. We have found that the electron flux in this region is associated with solar wind electron flux at a quarter of the proton frequency and is used to calculate the electron concentration in the E and F layers of the ionosphere. Our analysis shows that the calculated concentrations match observed values with an average difference of 300 km. We have also established a relationship between the ratio of solar wind electron concentration and ionospheric concentration and the effective height of the ionosphere, which is related to the latitude and solar activity.

In our research paper, we address a key problem in geographic information systems (GIS) - accurately predicting the point-of-attraction for a given location and text or image query. Unlike conventional text-based queries, which provide a clear description of the point-of-attraction, available data may lack the specific details required to accurately identify the location. To overcome this limitation, we've developed a novel approach that leverages both text and image data to predict the point-of-attraction. Our method involves using a pre-trained image encoder to extract features from the images, and then combining these features with text data using a transformer-based model, which we've adapted from the CLS paper. To evaluate our approach, we've developed a new dataset that includes 100k GPS-tagged images, and over 2000 points-of-interest, which we've annotated with both text and image descriptions. Our method significantly outperforms existing approaches, achieving a 0.7 increase in mean average precision.

This research paper delves into the post-call market performance of stocks listed on the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) following their quarterly conference calls, focusing on market fluctuations of $100 large-cap stocks listed on the exchange, analyzing their price movements in 2020 in response to COVID-19. The investigation reveals that stock prices tend to decline on the day of publication, stay volatile in the subsequent week, and return to pre-call levels in two weeks. Notably, the stock's market value before the call, rather than earnings, drives market movements after the call. The study also finds that the stock's market value following a call correlates with the frequency of participation in the earnings call, and that participation patterns are influenced by the pandemic.

In this research paper, we explore the problem of optimally placing sensors within a bounded area to efficiently collect and transmit spatial data to a central base-station using the minimum number of sensors possible.  To address this challenge, we have developed two novel placement strategies: one that utilizes uniform spacing and another that employs Chebyshev spacing for triangular and quadrilateral sensor layouts, respectively.  By distributing sensors in a uniform pattern, we can ensure that any point within the monitored area can be reached by at least one sensor with limited communication range, provided that that point is not more than 2r units away from any sensor.  Furthermore, we have developed a theoretical framework that demonstrates the effectiveness of our proposed sensor placement strategies.  The results of our numerical experiments confirm that our Chebyshev spacing approach outperforms traditional uniform placement strategies in terms of efficiency.

A novel quantum filtering method is introduced to estimate the average value of an unknown quantum state given noisy observations. The proposed filtering protocol utilizes a stream of single-mode measurements on a specific quantum state. A polynomial-based filter is derived and optimized to minimize estimation errors, and several key performance metrics are analyzed. The optimal filtering protocol exhibits enhanced performance compared to existing methods, notably outpacing the filtering tourney filter under certain conditions. The optimal filtering protocol also offers a means of optimal quantum linear algebra, where solving the resulting filter equations enables the most efficient quantum linear algebra approach.

We examine the behavior of compacton-type solutions in a $2d$ nonlinear electrodynamics infant skyrmion theory incorporating a $U(1)$ gauge field. This gauge field leads to the introduction of a new gauge-invariant variable, the current, which replaces the ordinary matter field in the original infant skyrmion model. We investigate compacton solutions in a neutral nonlinear electrodynamics medium and find that the presence of a $U(1)$ gauge field results in a $2\pi$ periodic current. We also discover that the current becomes a constant when a $U(1)$ gauge transformation is applied. Additionally, we analyze compacton solutions in a neutral nonlinear medium with a $U(1)$ gauge field and find that the presence of a magnetic field affects the current but not the compacton profile.

This report summarizes our efforts to investigate and expand the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) framework, particularly focusing on the development of novel SMEFT operators and their associated Wilson coefficients. We aimed to enhance the precision of our analysis by integrating cutting-edge experimental data from the LHC, as well as preparing the ground for future high-precision measurements at the $e^+e^-$ collider. By combining our expertise in global fits and collider studies, we have made significant strides in this field. Our achievements include the inclusion of two new SMEFT operators, the evaluation of their impacts on various observables, and the application of machine learning techniques to enhance our fits. We have also conducted a series of in-depth studies at the LHC and an early-stage assessment of the impact of certain SMEFT operators on the $e^+e^-$ collider's Higgs and top quark measurements.

We're introducing a diamond nuclear spin gyroscope based on nitrogen-vacancy centers that utilizes an innovative approach to rotation sensing. This device exploits the precession of nuclear spins in diamond, allowing for a stable and precise measurement of rotation. By combining optical detection of spin states with advanced pulse sequences, our gyroscope achieves high sensitivity and outperforms other diamond-based sensors. Following a detailed explanation of its operating principle and performance evaluation, our diamond nuclear spin gyroscope is showcased in a static display and we demonstrate its ability to accurately measure the speed of a rotating globe.

The development of whole-cell models is a complex task that requires a multidisciplinary approach, integrating various methods from the physical and biological sciences. Advances in experimental and computational technologies have made it possible to create models of cellular processes such as metabolism, regulation, and motility. However, a major challenge remains in creating comprehensive whole-cell models that can simulate the dynamic behavior of cells in response to various stimuli. This review provides an overview of the current state of whole-cell modeling, highlighting key principles and methods used in each stage of model development. Furthermore, it discusses the current progress in creating whole-cell models and identifies areas that require greater attention and collaboration from the scientific community.

We introduce Mobile Multi-View Object Picture Search, an innovative mobile application that empowers users to locate their object of interest within multiple pictures by utilizing a mobile device's camera and internet access. This application facilitates a comprehensive search strategy, effectively handling various query types, including those with low resolution, partial occlusions, and unfamiliar objects. Our novel system, implemented as a mobile web application, leverages a multi-view object database, comprising a large collection of objects across various perspectives. To address the distinct characteristics of mobile queries, we have devised a novel multi-view feature descriptor and a robust matching algorithm. This approach is capable of matching queries with relevant object views, even when the object is partially occluded or appears in low-resolution images. To enhance search accuracy further, we have incorporated a semi-supervised domain adaptation technique, allowing the system to adapt to its own performance and adapt to unfamiliar object categories. Our application has been thoroughly evaluated, demonstrating its superior performance in handling various search queries, including those with low-resolution images, and its ability to adapt to new object categories.

A cutting-edge approach to computing known as Hyperdimensional (HD) computing has shown potential in identifying seizures in individuals with epilepsy. This study investigates how various techniques used in HD computing, particularly hyperdimensional vector encoding and learning algorithms, affect seizure detection performance. We developed a system that utilizes HD computing to recognize seizure patterns, and we tested it using data collected from 22 patients who had undergone intracranial implantation as part of clinical research. Our results demonstrate that by integrating multiple strategies, including multiple patient data and hyperdimensional vector encoding, can significantly improve seizure detection accuracy. This is particularly true for short-term detection, as our proposed system achieved a high sensitivity of 93.7% and a low false alarm rate of 0.08 detections per hour.

The Vera Rubin Observatory's Deci-hertz Astrogravitational Observatory (DEAHO), which is under development, will be capable of detecting gravitational waves from binary black hole mergers at a frequency range of 1-10 Hz. This frequency range will enable the observation of gravitational waves from more distant binary black hole sources, which could serve as standard siren cosmological probes. We investigate the potential of DEAHO's binary black hole observations to improve the estimation of the Hubble constant, particularly in scenarios where the Hubble tension is resolved. We simulate the detection of binary black hole sources across a redshift range of 0.01-2.5 using a Fisher matrix analysis, assuming that DEAHO will detect 1000 binary black hole sources with Hubble tensions of 42.6 and 48.6 km/s/Mpc, respectively. We find that DEAHO's binary black hole observations will introduce significant uncertainties in the estimation of the Hubble constant, particularly for a Hubble tension of 42.6 km/s/Mpc, where the uncertainty will be approximately 4.4 km/s/Mpc. Conversely, for a Hubble tension of 48.6 km/s/Mpc, the uncertainty will be significantly larger, at approximately 16.5 km/s/Mpc.

We introduce QALD-9-plus, an expanded version of the DBpedia Question Answering dataset, comprising 1,094 questions in 10 languages, extensively annotated with detailed information, facilitating various QA system evaluations across multiple languages. This dataset is derived from QALD-9, a subset of the multilingual QA dataset, M-QA, which consists of questions in nine languages, along with corresponding reference answers. We refine this dataset by collecting additional relevant details from QA system developers and experts in linguistics, linguistics experts and QA developers. We also translate the questions into their respective languages using native speakers and validate the accuracy of the resulting answers. We then compare the performance of state-of-the-art QA systems on both QALD-9 and QALD-9-plus, revealing that the latter poses a more challenging evaluation for these systems. We provide access to the revised dataset, along with a comparative analysis of the results from the respective evaluations.

The human brain's ability to reevaluate and reclassify information is a crucial cognitive process, but current AI methods lack this capability, which is essential for tasks such as data reweighting and perception relabeling. We propose that the brain's ability to adapt and learn from experiences, through hindsight summation, underpins these processes, allowing it to update its internal model of the world. We model this cognitive mechanism as a strategy called Executive Function, a contrastive approach using information from the future to correct understanding of the past. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this strategy in a simulated environment and show its potential to improve AI performance on perception relabeling tasks.

Deep learning models in medical imaging have shown great promise, but their performance can be compromised by inherent biases present in the training data and deep learning architectures. To address this issue, we have developed an approach to identify biases within medical image datasets using a novel loss function that minimizes unwanted characteristics. This method is capable of handling both image-based and feature-based biases, as well as various neural network architectures. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to an in-house dataset of chest X-rays, which contains biases that affect both the image and feature domains. This approach enables data curators and scientists to assess and mitigate medical image dataset biases, ultimately enhancing the fairness of deep learning models in real-world clinical settings.

This paper tackles the issue of noisy labels in metric learning, where models trained on inaccurate metric loss can underperform on clean test data. Existing methods for addressing this problem have shown promise, but a key limitation is that they often overlook the fact that not all noisy labels have a comparable ground truth. We introduce a new approach called Smooth Proxy-Anchor Cost, or SPAce, which trains a signal detector to rank proxy-anchor pairs based on their similarity, then incorporates this ranking into the metric loss function. By doing so, SPAce enables the model to learn from noisy labels while avoiding the negative impact of incorrect rankings. The proposed method has been tested on various datasets and shows improved performance compared to other methods.

We introduce a novel statistical tool called the density weighted Pearson correlation function, known as $rp_\omega(\theta)$, which is an extension of the conventional Pearson correlation function. This function takes into consideration the spatial distribution of galaxy samples by assigning a weight based on the spatial variance of galaxies. We explore the potential of using $rp_\omega(\theta)$ to study the properties of the universe by analyzing the spatial distribution of galaxies within different cosmological models. We use the MultiDark-Patchy simulation to study the spatial characteristics of galaxies in an empty universe and how they change when dark matter particles are introduced. We find that the function $rp_\omega(\theta)$ is more sensitive to changes in the mass of dark matter particles and the amplitude of matter fluctuations. We also find that the function $rp_\omega(\theta)$ is more robust to changes in the spatial distribution of galaxies than the conventional Pearson correlation function. We conclude that $rp_\omega(\theta)$ can be used to study the spatial distribution of galaxies in various cosmological models and can be used to constrain cosmological parameters. We also find that the function $rp_\omega(\theta)$ can be used to distinguish between different cosmological models, such as the Lambda cold dark matter model and the modified gravity model, using the data from the SDSS DR12. A theoretical model of a $^3$He-$^4$e$^-$ compound fermion is proposed to describe the topological SO(5) superfluidity in $^3$He-$^4$e$^-$ pairs within a quantum fluid. This compound fermion is composed of a $^3$He spinor and a $^4$He atom accompanied by an electron, which combines their properties through a Feshbach coupling. Theoretical analysis of the superfluid phase diagram reveals a complex interplay between the $^3$He superfluid order parameter and the $^4$He dipolar polarization, leading to the emergence of a topological superfluid with exotic properties. Theoretical findings suggest that the superfluid's gapless Dirac points can be experimentally detected by utilizing a $^3^4$He$^-$ mixture of $^3$He-$^4$He-$^-$ pairs in a confined medium.

Phosphor-converted MAPD type photodetectors are designed to be highly sensitive, with low sensitivity to the surrounding optical noise. When a MAPD with a phosphor is excited by a light signal, the phosphor converts the photons into electron-excited pulses that are read out by an integrated readout ASIC. This noise-free photodetector is suitable for applications in small and compact light detection systems. This paper discusses the development of a noise-free photodetector with a snowstorm type phosphor, which is achieved by depositing the phosphor onto the MAPD's active area. This photodetector is highly sensitive, with a sensitivity of around 10 electrons per photon, with low noise levels. This highly sensitive photodetector is suitable for applications in small light detection systems such as single photon detection and imaging.

This research introduces the concept of curved Sectors and explores their properties, as well as associated curved Ext modules and their structures. We examine the characteristics of curved Ext modules over commutative rings with an ideal of finite generation depth, and establish connections to Gorenstein and Cohen-Macaulay modules. Additionally, we define the curved Hilbert series of a curved Ext module and discuss relationships with the Gorenstein and Cohen-Macaulay cases.

A comprehensive study of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO) was conducted using nuclear forward scattering (NFS) to monitor structural changes and magnetic order at elevated pressures. BFTO's crystal structure, which is a distorted Aurivillius type, was studied under pressures ranging from 0.4 to 2.1 GPa. NFS measurements indicated a non-magnetic state at low pressures, which was confirmed by neutron diffraction. However, at 1.9 GPa and temperatures between 295 and 360 K, BFTO exhibited long-range magnetic ordering. This transition was attributed to increased oxygen mobility, which was further confirmed by a similar phase transition observed in oxygen isotope exchange experiments. NFS measurements also showed that this magnetic state persisted until 1.6 GPa and a temperature of 360 K, beyond which it disappeared. Notably, BFTO's magnetic ordering was observed to increase with pressure and temperature, which was further confirmed by a linear relationship between magnetic ordering and both pressure and temperature. This study's NFS results are supported by density functional theory (DFT) calculations, which were used to predict the phase diagram of BFTO.

To provide investors with an informed decision about choosing broker algorithms, we have developed a method for quantifying the impact of trading costs. Leveraging a Bayesian framework, we create a probabilistic model that estimates trading expenses by simulating transactions and calculating execution costs. This model is then applied to real-world market data and used to analyze the trading behavior of brokers, ultimately enabling investors to compare and select the most cost-effective options.

We have developed a comprehensive model for a highly adaptable optomechanical filter that can be used in add-drop configurations. This model takes into account the effects of mechanical loss, intracavity power, and the relationship between the optical modes' frequencies and refractive indices. Using this model, we calculated the transmission loss of add-drop filters at various frequencies and parameter settings. Our results show that even with mechanical loss considered, the transmission loss of these filters can be negligible at high power levels, given a specific adjustment range of 0.1% optical coupling strength.

Public health interventions are developed in response to emerging infectious disease threats such as COVID-19, with the goal of minimizing their spread. These interventions, including social distancing and quarantine procedures, are implemented with the aim of protecting human life and maintaining economic stability. As a result, there is a pressing need to assess the potential effectiveness of different interventions in various contexts, including locations with distinct cultural, economic, and geographical profiles. Researchers have proposed the use of data from social media to evaluate these interventions, with the assumption that the content posted can be used to infer the behavior of the general population. This approach has been applied to social media platforms such as Twitter, with the goal of modeling the potential impact of different interventions on the spread of an outbreak. However, the existing methods for evaluating these interventions have several limitations, including a reliance on biased data and the use of assumptions that may not be applicable in all cases. This research aims to address these limitations by presenting a new framework for evaluating public health interventions that utilizes data from social media to estimate the behavior of individuals. This framework is designed to be more accurate and reliable than existing methods by accounting for biases in the data and using more realistic assumptions about human behavior.

This research focuses on developing highly efficient algorithms for lossless image compression, utilizing the latest GPU technology. By combining an advanced neural network architecture with a specific encoding technique, we've achieved a compression efficiency that outperforms existing methods. Our results demonstrate superior performance on various datasets, including the Urban100 benchmark, with significant compression ratios of 1.38 bits per pixel and 2.5% in overall rate-distortion.

The LHCb experiment observed its first instance of the $B^{+}$ decaying into $D_s^{+}K^{+}K^{-}$ for the first time using data collected in 2011 from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. With a collected data set of 1 fb$^{-1}$, the experiment determined the branching fraction for this reaction, finding $\mathcal{B}(B^{+} \to D_s^{+}K^{+}K^{-}) = (7.1 \pm 0.4 \pm 0.3) \times 10^{-4}$. The experiment also conducted a search for $B^{+} \to D_s^{+}\phi$ decays and established the branching fraction for this reaction at $\mathcal{B}(B^{+} \to D_s^{+}\phi) = (2.46 \pm 0.54 \pm 0.16 \pm 0.17) \times 10^{-3}$.

Optimal transport has seen significant use in various machine learning applications.  However, its vulnerability to outliers poses a significant challenge.  To address this, we have developed a robust framework that effectively mitigates the impact of such data anomalies.  By leveraging the concept of an integral shift in the dual representation, we have formulated a novel formulation that is capable of detecting outliers across both synthetic and real-world datasets.  Notably, our approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods, including robust loss functions and outlier detection techniques, as demonstrated through a series of experiments.

In order to achieve true collaboration, artificial intelligence agents must be able to put the collective goals of their teammates first, rather than just their own success. This requires agents to be able to work in harmony with their teammates by anticipating their actions, making strategic decisions, and coordinating their own actions to maximize the benefits for the entire team. In our research, we've developed a framework that allows for the creation of a collaborative human-AI team agent, which we've tested in a dynamic scenario that requires rapid planning and quick reflexes. Our results show that when working together, the AI teammate and its human partner can solve complex problems more efficiently than a single human could have managed alone. Furthermore, we've found that by leveraging the strengths of both the human and AI components, the team was able to make more collaborative and effective decisions than either component could have made alone. This was particularly evident in the team's ability to balance its own goals with its partner's actions, demonstrating a high level of synergy and true collaboration.

We have developed a computational tool called HeavySpectrums that can automatically determine the dimensions of supersymmetry parameters in supersymmetric models, taking into account any number of additional gauge groups, scalar fields, and mirror families. HeavySpectrums enables the automatic generation of mass terms, Lagrangian terms, and Wilson operators, making it a valuable asset for phenomenological studies, pedagogy, and educational purposes. HeavySpectrums is freely available as an open-source Python package and processing can be accessed online.

Visualizing intricate datasets is a key aspect of communication between data analysts and various industries, and the use of visualizations has become widespread across different sectors. Despite this, little research has been conducted to determine which types of visualizations are most effective for specific fields, and whether certain fields require unique approaches to visualization due to their distinct backgrounds and knowledge bases. In an effort to address this knowledge gap, we conducted a survey of 200 individuals from three distinct fields - computer science, marketing, and medicine - and administered a series of tasks to assess their ability to effectively use various types of visualizations. The results of this study, which were based on the performance of 61 individuals across the three fields on 12 different tasks, revealed that there were significant differences in the ability of individuals from different disciplines to effectively use visualizations, and these results also highlighted the importance of considering the background and knowledge base of individuals when designing visualizations.

We introduce a novel framework for verifying inductive correctness of loop programs that incorporate user-defined assertions using a set of axiomatic formulas. The verification process relies on three main elements: an inductive proof of the assertions, a manual analysis of the loop's body, and an inductive framework for the axiomatic formulas. The inductive framework is established by representing the axiomatic formulas as transition systems, allowing for a more intuitive understanding of the loop invariants. The approach is demonstrated through a specific example, where a cell phone protocol is shown to be correctly implemented using a set of axiomatic formulas.

Graph retrieval is a growing field of study in natural language processing, drawing from information retrieval and natural language understanding. In this paper, we explore the link between graph retrieval and natural language retrieval, highlighting the similarity between retrieval and classification tasks in natural language understanding. We demonstrate that a corresponding text classification model can be used for graph retrieval through node embedding and classification, and experimentally verify this connection using standard text classification models and datasets such as TREC6, AGNEWS, and SQUAD.

Deep learning techniques have been extensively researched for transient dynamics modeling, but most of these methods focus solely on training. We argue that training procedures and evaluation metrics are just as crucial as novel model architectures. Drawing from advancements in natural language processing, we introduce a novel training technique known as "warm-up" for physics-informed learning. Warm-up involves gradual reduction of a term that aligns the model with its underlying physics. We demonstrate that warm-up overcomes the limitations of conventional loss functions, which can hinder transient dynamics modeling. Additionally, we propose a more efficient evaluation metric, mean absolute error per degree of freedom, to facilitate comparison of training procedures.

A fair distribution of electricity costs, where total costs are evenly split among all users, is often not the most suitable goal due to varying usage levels among users. The concept of cost-per-unit pricing exists to incentivize energy conservation, but it poses a challenge when allocating historical bills to users, as it rewards those who consume more. To address this issue, we develop new methods to fairly distribute total costs based on actual usage patterns. We frame this task as a joint distribution and allocation problem and propose a robust algorithm that maintains cost-per-unit pricing while ensuring fairness. We conduct a thorough theoretical analysis and experimentally validate our approach in real-world scenarios, showcasing its effectiveness over current methods.

The task of coreference resolution in news events seeks to identify and connect mentions referencing the same real-world occurrence. This research tackles this challenge by employing a multi-stage approach that leverages a combination of BERT-based classification and fine-tuning of pre-trained entity embeddings. We evaluate our method on multiple event datasets, focusing particularly on a novel dataset encompassing 20,000 news articles related to contentious political events. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the efficacy of our multi-stage strategy, which surpasses the performance of earlier approaches.

A novel polyhedral representation has been developed for the complementarity knapsack problem polytope, denoted as $P_2\overline{K}_n$, through the construction of a novel extension of the cross polytope. This representation, introduced in a recent study, has been utilized to derive tight facet-defining inequalities with non-zero coefficients for the first time within the context of complementarity knapsack problems. Additionally, it has been possible to identify novel inequalities with zero coefficients that define facets of the $P_2\overline{K}_n$ polytope.
This article establishes the concept of generalized $(m, n)$-Jordan derivations and centralizers, and investigates their properties within semiprime rings.
We demonstrate that Weinberg's two-parameter strong interaction low-energy theorem can be derived solely from the helicity decomposition principles in quantum field theory.

We explore families of nonlinear transformations that link finite-dimensional spaces, focusing on their transversality and Favard length. This work extends the Favard length formula from linear to nonlinear transformations, while introducing new definitions for transversality and Favard length formulas when the initial space is infinite-dimensional.

We introduce a novel, efficient guided policy search method, called Tube-guided Policy Search (T-PS), to resolve the issue of transferring a model-based controller to a black-box policy. T-PS generates policies that closely resemble the optimal feedback control strategy of the original model-based controller while minimizing the number of demonstration trajectories required. The policy is optimized by incorporating a tube constraint, which restricts the distance between the current state and the future states within a pre-defined tube. The policy is then updated by solving a sequential tube maximum a posteriori (TMAP) problem, which involves a tube-based safety constraint. The safety constraint is relaxed to solve a modified problem, called the safe tube MAP problem, which is solved using a forward-backward algorithm. The algorithm involves a forward prediction step, followed by a backward optimization step. The safety constraint is then released, and the policy is updated using the sequential T-MAP problem. The policy is then evaluated on a set of trajectories, and the worst-case cost is used as the objective function for the policy update. The policy is then updated using gradient descent, which is applied to the policy parameters using the gradient of the worst-case cost. The algorithm involves a forward-backward pass to compute the gradient of the worst-case cost. The policy is then updated using the gradient descent algorithm. Recent experiments have found unusual intrinsic Hall components in 2D materials.  This unusual effect originates from the spin-orbit interaction and specific band structures.  This study examines the unusual intrinsic Hall effect up to its third order using a semiclassical theory that generalizes the Berry phase approach.  The results show that the leading order of this unusual Hall effect is related to the curvature of the energy bands and the circularity of the Fermi surface.  The second-order is related to the curvature and ferromagnetic properties, while the third-order is related to the curvature, spin-orbit interaction, and ferromagnetic properties.  This study provides a theoretical basis for the identification of the third-order unusual intrinsic Hall effect in future experiments.

Call graphs are a valuable resource for software maintenance by providing call graph summaries and call tree maps to highlight call graph characteristics. However, as summaries are often generic and map views are call graph-specific, it can be challenging to compare collections of call graphs in a comprehensive manner. In this paper, we introduce an innovative method for visually analyzing multiple call graphs within a single visual display. This method can be applied to various call graph types, including composite call graphs, and can accommodate a large number of call graphs. A user study validates the method's effectiveness and potential for use in both call graph analysis and software maintenance.

The "No News is Positive News" dataset, a widely used resource in natural language processing (NLP) for measuring text quality, has significant flaws that affect its performance in predicting text quality. Our analysis reveals that this benchmark is plagued by numerous errors, leading to inconsistent and inaccurate results when evaluating text quality. Our investigation into these issues sheds light on the underlying causes and proposes a simple method to address them. Moreover, we demonstrate that the same issues affect other related benchmarks and discuss the broader implications for the field of NLP that arise from these errors.

The formation of magnetic field structures in solar and stellar flares is linked to the development of current sheets. This process can be influenced by quasi-periodic oscillations, leading to the creation of magnetic islands that emit radio waves. Our research involves using 3D particle-in-cell simulations to model the formation of current sheets and observe the development of quasi-periodic oscillations, magnetic islands, and radio emission. Our findings indicate that magnetic islands emit radio waves, which are detectable by radio telescopes, allowing us to analyze the radio dynamic spectra of these events. This analysis reveals that the oscillations produce a characteristic shape in the radio waves, known as a drift spectrum, with a narrow band at the oscillation frequency and broader bands at higher frequencies. This pattern is related to the oscillation amplitude and period, allowing us to derive an empirical formula for predicting the oscillation frequency. Our results also show that the oscillations can produce a characteristic shape in the radio waves, known as a drift strip spectrum, with a single strip at the oscillation frequency and broader strips at higher frequencies. This pattern is related to the oscillation period and magnetic field strength, allowing us to derive an empirical formula for predicting the oscillation frequency. Our research has the potential to inform the development of future radio observatories, such as the Square Kilometre Array, which will enable the detection of these events.

This paper presents a novel approach for anomaly detection in visual inspection applications, characterized by high throughput and efficient multi-scale analysis. The proposed method addresses a common challenge in the manufacturing industry, where products undergo quality control prior to assembly, and operators manually inspect them to identify defects, a time-consuming and labor-intensive task. To improve efficiency, existing systems integrate machine vision technology, and this work aims to enhance the detection capabilities by employing a multi-scale analysis. At each scale, a feature vector is generated from the input image, and a one-class support vector machine is trained to identify anomalies. A cost function is then formulated to optimize the detection performance through an iterative process. Validation tests on the well-known KPII dataset have confirmed the method's effectiveness.
We demonstrate the global existence of low-regularity solutions to the KP-I equation with a general dispersion term. This builds upon prior work for specific dispersion cases.

Kramer's theorem establishes the degeneracy of non-interacting spin-1/2 systems' energy levels, an effect that remains intact in isolated quantum systems. However, this work reveals that Kramer's degeneracy is not a universal invariant when the system is exposed to environmental influences. We find that energy level degeneracy can be broken down by external influences but will be restored once these influences cease, an effect observed in both a basic model and real-world scenarios.

Achieving accurate channel state information (CSI) is essential for enabling massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems to function optimally. However, this goal becomes particularly challenging in highly mobile scenarios where the pre-coded channel responses deviate from the actual future CSI responses. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel method that utilizes a combination of long short-term memory (LSTM) and bidirectional autoencoders to predict future CSI responses. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a comprehensive analysis of its performance under various conditions. The results show that the proposed LSTM-AE model can achieve an average mean squared error of 0.0351, indicating its potential to predict future CSI responses with high accuracy. This accuracy enables the LSTM-AE model to significantly reduce the overhead associated with CSI feedback, thereby allowing the system to function within its designed specifications even at high signal-to-noise ratios.

This paper explores the use of small sample size datasets to assess and analyze inequality in microdata. We introduce a novel method for estimating generalized inequality parameters, leveraging the fact that they can be seen as special cases of mixture distributions of beta components. Our approach is compared to existing methods through Monte Carlo simulations under varying data conditions, and its efficacy is demonstrated on real-world datasets from Kenya and Tanzania.

We establish an asymptotic expansion for the Szeg\H{o} kernel on complex Grauert cylinders, leveraging the scaling method, while obtaining a more precise estimate using the subprincipal term. This is achieved under the condition that the underlying pseudoconvex domain has a boundary of finite holomorphic slope.

This research paper presents a novel algorithm called MARINLINGA, a tool that efficiently generates reverse line graphs from original graphs. MARINLINGA's algorithm is straightforward and operates in a single pass through the original graph's edges, making it a fast computation method. MARINLINGA also offers flexibility in handling graphs with duplicate edges, either merging or counting them as needed. MARINLINGA's algorithm is further compared to Roussopoulos's approach, showing that both can produce isomorphic reverse line graphs. An advantage of MARINLINGA over Roussopoulos's method is its reduced computational time, specifically O(ve + ec) compared to O(ve). Additionally, MARINLINGA's algorithm is capable of producing a reverse line graph with a lower number of edges, often resulting in fewer edges by 50%.

This paper validates a conjecture proposed by Lee-Lee, which pertains to the intrinsic structure of rigid modules within the limited linear context, and provides an explicit description of the associated graded modules in the filtration of maps generated by automorphisms.

The Java Virtual Machine's widespread adoption has led to a surge in complex, interconnected software ecosystems. Although these ecosystems bring numerous benefits, they also introduce significant risks by introducing security vulnerabilities and impeding project development. Our investigation into the Java ecosystem, spanning nearly 15 years, reveals a dramatic expansion of dependency networks, with a substantial number of redundant and underutilized dependencies. Our findings suggest that nearly a quarter of dependencies are used by only a single project, and nearly half of dependencies are linked to a single lead developer. Our analysis also highlights a rise in long-term dependency commitment, decreased dependency duration, and increased likelihood of dependency removal. These trends underscore the complexity and vulnerability of modern Java software ecosystems, and provide valuable insights for informing developers, identifying vulnerabilities, and guiding strategic downstream decisions.

In an entangled biphoton system, entanglement plays a crucial role in quantum information processing through various methods. One such method involves the use of entanglement as a resource to create a controlled state, where the goal is to produce a desired state by manipulating the entanglement. However, this process can be hindered by errors that stem from the imperfect behavior of particles in the entangled biphoton when interacting with other particles. Researchers have discovered that the presence of residual entanglement in the medium can either aid or impede the desired state creation, depending on the specific degree of entanglement present. This discovery has significant implications for understanding the complex dynamics of entanglement in quantum systems, where the behavior of entangled photons can either reinforce or undermine the creation of a controlled state, highlighting the delicate and often conflicting nature of entanglement in quantum processes.

We develop a framework to identify and select the most impactful scenarios in multistage optimization under uncertainty, where distributional relationships are considered. The proposed situation selection process leverages an information gain metric derived from conditional Kullback-Leibler divergence to choose scenarios based on their distance from a reference distribution. This method is extended to accommodate various metrics, including total variation distance. To improve computational efficiency, a lower bound is developed for the optimal solution of the main optimization problem, allowing for an approximate situation selection process. The proposed framework is applied to a two-stage optimization problem with a budgeted scenario selection problem and demonstrated through numerical experiments.

Predicting actions based on observations is a crucial task in various robotic applications, encompassing scenarios from autonomous driving to robotic manipulation. In this paper, we introduce a sophisticated predictive model that effectively forecasts actions by utilizing a feature mapping function with an RBF kernel in conjunction with an encoder-decoder framework powered by recurrent neural networks. This approach enables the model to learn long-term relationships and accurately capture the essence of sequential data, thereby generating a more comprehensive representation of future actions. Furthermore, an innovative loss function is proposed to mitigate the issue of vanishing gradients during backpropagation, which occurs when forecasting distant actions. Our proposed model is evaluated using two publicly accessible datasets, demonstrating significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods, particularly when predicting actions at a greater distance.

We have developed a method to achieve deep thermalization in a quantum system that starts in a particular state and is influenced by a time-dependent Hamiltonian. Our approach involves a technique known as the Adiabatic Perturbation Theory, and it allows us to break down the thermalization process into distinct stages. By applying this method, we were able to derive a framework for analyzing and understanding the thermalization of complex quantum systems, as well as providing a concrete example to demonstrate its efficacy.

We establish a criterion for the boundedness of pseudo-differential operators on uniform tree structures and create a method to calculate their Weyl transform, which is proven to be bounded under a specific condition. Additionally, we demonstrate that the Weyl transform corresponds to a compact operator if and only if a particular property is met, and in a uniform tree setting, this property is equivalent to the operator's invariance. Lastly, we show that the Weyl transform of a uniform tree pseudo-differential operator is nuclear if and only if its partial trace on a specific leaf space is a compact operator.

The rapid expansion of 5G networks has led to widespread adoption of mobile devices. This research investigates the relative prominence of smartphones in 5G mobile networks, comparing their performance with that of other types of devices using a single network. The study found that when rules are applied, devices other than smartphones account for only a small fraction of total traffic, with an average of 0.2% indicating minimal impact. The data further suggests that with network restrictions in place, smartphone traffic increases by 7.7 times, resulting in them dominating traffic by approximately 93.6%. The findings also show that when devices are not subject to data limits, their traffic remains consistent at a low level, with an average of 0.2% in all cases. The results indicate that when data is not limited, devices other than smartphones account for most traffic, with an average of 99.7%, and smartphone traffic increases by approximately 16.8 times, resulting in smartphones dominating traffic by approximately 93.2%.

Deep neural networks struggle with accurately predicting novel and unforeseen inputs. This challenge stems from a common problem known as overconfidence, where these networks tend to generate overly optimistic predictions for out-of-distribution data. This phenomenon can be attributed to the distinct characteristics of in- and out-of-distribution data within a specific feature space. This work presents a new approach called $CODES$, an innovative method for identifying out-of-distribution data, based on the analysis of the convergence of the two nearest neighbors in the feature space. By utilizing the convergence of the two nearest neighbors in the feature space, $CODES$ is able to effectively distinguish in- and out-of-distribution data, achieving superior performance compared to existing methods.

The CMS experiment at the LHC has studied the relationships between the parts of collisions between protons, where the parts are classified based on the number of jets. These studies were done using data from collisions at an extremely high energy level of 13 teraelectronvolts. The data used were collected over a period of time and amount to an integrated luminosity of nearly 36 inverse femtobarns. The relationships between the parts of collisions, measured in degrees, were found to be distributed uniformly around the direct collision axis. The measurements were done with a high level of accuracy and amount, and amount to the most accurate measurements of these relationships up to this point in the research. The relationships between the parts of collisions, when broken down into two types, were also found to be in agreement with predictions made by a computer program that uses the next leading order of quantum chromodynamics. These studies were done without the use of any prior knowledge of the relationships between the parts of collisions, and amount, and amount to the most accurate measurements of these relationships up to this point in the research. The studies were also found to be in agreement with predictions made by a computer program that uses the next leading order of quantum chromodynamics.
