We demonstrate that the trained model can be used to make more informed predictions by selecting a specific quantile or moment of the resulting distribution. Our method is applied to regression tasks and binary classification tasks and is found to outperform existing methods in terms of uncertainty quantification.

The Marcus-Levich-Jortner theory is a widely accepted concept in chemistry that describes electron transfer events at high temperatures. It suggests an activation energy of $E_A = \Gamma$, with $\Gamma$ representing the thermal energy of the acceptor. This theory is based on the idea that only the real part of the off-diagonal element of the Hamiltonian is considered when evaluating the rate of electron transfer, with the real part of the on-diagonal element of the Hamiltonian acting as a factor. This simplified view is analogous to a semiclassical approximation where the diagonal element is treated as a static potential and the off-diagonal element is treated as a momentum operator. This approximation can be represented as an instanton solution of a Schrödinger equation with a cubic potential, resulting in $E_A = \Gamma$ at high temperatures. However, as temperatures decrease, the instanton solution becomes a saddle point of the cubic potential, leading to an activation energy of $E_A = \Gamma - \sqrt{\Gamma^2 - \Delta}$, with $\Delta$ representing the gap between the HOMO and LEMO of the donor. This expression for $E_A$ is consistent with the Marcus-Levich-Jortner theory.

This research introduces a methodology for designing trajectory tracking control systems from scratch, incorporating multiple components that work in tandem to achieve accurate tracking, stability, and robustness, utilizing a variety of mathematical tools. A specific case study involving a broom-ing robot exemplifies this approach.

A theoretical framework for the thermoelectric effect in its broad sense has been developed based on the magnon drag mechanism. This framework involves the use of the Boltzmann equation, in conjunction with the relaxation time approximation, to describe the thermopower and heat conductivity under conditions of thermal gradient. The theoretical model takes into account the distinct thermal effects of charge and spin carriers and incorporates the effects of thermal asymmetry and carrier interactions. This framework was applied to the case of a thin film of the ferromagnetic alloy Fe$_{81}$Co$_{19}$, in which the thermal drag generated by magnon drag was found to be comparable to that produced by the ordinary drag mechanism. The theoretical model was also used to investigate the effects of layer thickness and temperature on the thermoelectric properties of the alloy.

The problem of perfect sum, initially introduced by Nivas R. Das and S. Chakravarthy in 1989, is a complex problem within the realm of integer programming and combinatorial optimization. It seeks the minimum number of items from given sets, each containing unique items, that can collectively sum up to a predetermined target value. Despite its extensive practical applications across various fields, a solution to this problem remains elusive. This study aims to investigate a probabilistic method for finding the optimal solution to the perfect sum problem. This method is based on the premise that the minimum number of items required to achieve a perfect sum is equivalent to the number of items needed to achieve a perfect sum in a modified set of items, where each item's value is randomly selected from the original set. This method is then applied to the perfect sum problem using a greedy algorithm. This study also presents a novel approach for determining the optimal number of items using a modified set of items. This method is based on the concept of partitioning the range of target values into intervals and selecting a representative item from each interval. This study also provides a probabilistic method for determining the optimal number of items using a modified set of items. This method is based on the concept of using a greedy algorithm to select items from each interval. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of these approaches through numerical examples.

This work provides an in-depth analysis of finite fields with a specific type of structure, determined by a particular equation. By applying a well-established method from algebraic geometry, it systematically computes the key properties of this structured class of fields. These properties include measures of complexity, like the size of specific groups, and other notable elements, like the highest ordered values, which hold significant importance. The method initially provides a general explanation, followed by detailed calculations for fields with smaller dimensions, illustrating its applicability and significance.

This study proposes an innovative method for exploring source code through the lens of reactive synthesis, leveraging the powerful tools of UPPAAL, a renowned model checking software. Our approach is demonstrated by synthesizing executable code from a given source code structure, ensuring it meets specific requirements, and all aspects of the code are properly connected. We also highlight the potential for this concept to be applied in other contexts, such as automatically generating test suites for complex functions.

A novel imaging technique utilizes a metasurface to capture scattered data from an object's surface features. The metasurface acts as a 2D array sensor, where each element can be customized to enhance particular spectral or phase characteristics. Although the potential of metasurface-based sensors is promising, their practical implementation faces challenges stemming from manufacturing and design uncertainties. A new method has been developed to address these issues by integrating compressed sensing with a closed-loop optimization technique. The technique allows for the simultaneous optimization and characterization of metasurface elements, ultimately leading to improved image quality. A comprehensive study of metasurface performance metrics, such as reflection, absorption, and phase characteristics, has been conducted using a non-invasive optimization technique. The findings demonstrate the potential of the proposed approach to achieve high-quality imaging with significantly reduced reconstruction errors.

We have observed a shift in the spectral pattern of the Balmer-alpha spectral line when it's exposed to two highly polarized laser fields. By analyzing how the line's structure changes in response to varying laser intensities, we were able to identify distinct regions where the line splits into multiple peaks. This occurs due to the unique interaction between the line's core and the ac-Stark-shifted frequencies of the laser fields, which enables the excitation of specific Rydberg states. Furthermore, our research reveals that the line's core can give rise to a multitude of peaks, which we have found to occur at varying laser intensities. This phenomenon allows us to precisely determine the positions of the ac-Stark-shifted frequencies and their associated intensities, which we have validated through theoretical calculations.

We introduce an innovative approach to blending images by directly exchanging meaningful aspects. In contrast to conventional methods, the system first identifies and swaps the semantic elements (diverting from the original) before applying a series of regularizers to preserve the integrity of the resulting images. The system iteratively refines and improve the results by optimizing these regularizers. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through various experiments, outperforming other methods in producing high-quality mixed images with distinct characteristics.

The expression of genes in living organisms is represented as a time series of discrete values over time.  The traditional approach to studying gene expression is based on analyzing these time series at specific time points, but this method neglects the potential for extracting meaningful information from the intermediate periods between measurements.  In this study, we investigate the use of gene expression data as a stochastic process to uncover previously unreported characteristics of genetic regulation.  We have developed a computational method that can be used to identify the underlying probability distribution of gene expression, as well as the specific parameters that govern this process.  Our results show that the method accurately predicts the underlying probability distribution of gene expression in individual cells, and can also be used to identify key regulatory elements in a given set of genes.  The precision of the method was evaluated by comparing the results to established knowledge of gene regulation and by assessing the sensitivity of the method to variations in the underlying data.  The method was applied to a set of genes in the E. coli bacterium and was found to provide a more accurate representation of gene regulation than existing models, which are based on analyzing discrete snapshots of gene expression levels.

A fundamental challenge in machine learning is creating effective models from limited labeled data. In order to address this, we've developed a semi-supervised learning method grounded in the principles of self-training. By leveraging vast amounts of unlabeled data, our approach learns from these sources and refines the model's embedding capabilities through a process involving pseudo-label generation, data transformation, and density estimation. The performance of our method has been evaluated by applying it to various classification tasks across multiple datasets, including those from the MNIST, CIFAR-10/100, and WebVision datasets, with our method demonstrating notable improvements over conventional semi-supervised learning techniques.

The process of layer-by-layer training for variational quantum eigenstate solving, also known as saturation, is explored in this study. We examine the characteristics of saturation, identify its key features, and provide evidence of three distinct saturation types. Our research further reveals that the expected energy value remains stable over time, and we introduce a new, efficient method for determining the point at which layer-by-layer training reaches saturation. Our experimental data, conducted on a IBM quantum device, supports the validity of our theoretical findings.

In the context of distributed learning, a number of users contribute local models to a shared platform. The platform aggregates and updates these models to provide the collective knowledge to its users. We investigate the vulnerability of this training process to adversarial attacks that aim to expose the individual models, specifically in terms of re-identifying the associated user data. We introduce a new metric, called the Re-Identification Score, to quantify this risk and demonstrate its effectiveness in detecting re-identification attacks. Our results show that this metric accurately measures the vulnerability of training processes to various attacks that exploit public shared data.

To accurately model and forecast future power grids, time series data must be effectively analyzed. However, the complexity and variability inherent in grid operations often result in datasets that are difficult to interpret. As modern power grids increasingly rely on renewable energy sources and smart devices, the data required to study them is vast and intricate. This paper introduces a comprehensive framework for analyzing time series data, enabling researchers to extract meaningful insights from complex datasets and reproduce results efficiently. The framework's capabilities include data visualization, statistical analysis, and simulation replication. A practical demonstration is provided using the IEEE 33-bus and 68-bus systems, showcasing the framework's applicability to diverse power system configurations. The framework's open-source code is publicly accessible on GitHub.

Let $\left( X, \left\| \cdot \right\| \right)$ be a real Banach space, and the set $A$ be a nonempty subset of the dual space $X^*$. We consider a function $F: A \to \mathbb{R}$ that is continuous and monotone, and a sequence of points $\{x_n\}_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ in $A$ that fulfills a specific inequality condition. We aim to demonstrate that, under these conditions, the sequence $\{x_n\}_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ converges uniquely to the solution of a particular variational inequality problem.

A Fuchsian group, denoted by $\Gamma$, is classified as isoxial if it possesses a finite index subgroup $\widetilde{\Gamma}$, which is equivalent to $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$, allowing us to establish several distinct criteria for determining whether $\Gamma$ allows the presence of two geodesic simple crossings within the Poincar\'{e} half-plane $\mathbb{H}$.

The $\Upsilon(3S)$ decay process $\Upsilon(3S) \to e^\pm \mu^{\mp}$ was investigated at a center-of-mass energy of 9.86 GeV using data collected by the BESIII detector, resulting in an observed branching fraction of $3.0\times 10^{-6}$ with a statistical error of $0.6\times 10^{-6}$. This branching fraction is in agreement with the prediction of the Standard Model, according to the CLEO measurement of $1.0\times 10^{-6}$. The $\Upsilon(3S)$ decay process $e^\pm \mu^{\mp}$ is the first instance where a lepton flavor violating decay has been observed in charmonium particles.

The Kagome lattice, a fundamental structure in many quantum materials, is also the foundation for a unique flat-band system. This flat-band system is characterized by localized and extended states that coexist and exhibit distinct characteristics. Despite the theoretical significance, experimental evidence for a pressure-induced flat-band superconductivity has proven elusive. Our research on Pd$_3$P$_2$(S$_1-x$Se$_x$)$_8$ has led to the discovery of a pressure-induced superconductivity at low temperatures, occurring at pressures of 1.5 kbar and above. Notably, the superconducting critical temperature increases with pressure, a phenomenon observed in both Pd$_3$P$_2$S$_8$ and Pd$_3$P$_2$Se$_8$. Our findings suggest that the superconductivity arises from the application of pressure, rather than changes in the chemical composition. Notably, the superconducting transition pressure is insensitive to the sulfur-selenium composition, a phenomenon that cannot be explained by a simple alloy effect. Our results indicate that the superconductivity arises from the application of pressure, leading to the flattening of the band structure.

We investigate the recovery of black hole data from linear combinations of Hawking modes using the 0-form and vector scalar-JT gravity. By combining the Hawking modes with a set of boundary operators, we find that the overlap between these modes and the boundary operators determines a set of inner product coefficients. We then derive a formula to compute the inner product of the boundary operators using the conformal field theory correlation functions. We use this formula to study the recovery of black hole data in the presence of arbitrary boundary operators. We also examine the scenario where the boundary is deformed and analyze the robustness of the inner product against such deformations.

The increasing availability of high-resolution data from sensors and other sources has led to a surge in demand for models that can effectively utilize these large datasets. Unfortunately, many high-resolution models are restricted by their requirement for data that must be precisely measured and consistently available. In contrast, certain models such as Neural SDEs can effectively handle noisy data, but they must be based on a fundamental Markov-Process. In this study, we introduce a novel approach called Neural SDE with jumps, which can handle data with significant temporal variations without compromising its accuracy. Our model builds on Neural SDEs by incorporating a jump process that can effectively handle non-smooth functions, and we utilize a continuous-time autoregressive process to model the jumps. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach can effectively model data with temporal variations and that it provides a more accurate representation of the data than traditional Neural SDEs.

Current navigation algorithms in robotics often struggle to remember previously seen objects, hindering their ability to navigate to multiple targets. To address this, we developed an end-to-end transformer-based model called Object Recall Transformer (ORT), designed to recall objects at specific locations in the scene. Unlike current methods, ORT identifies objects without bounding box coordinates, instead using object labels and 3D scene information. When tested on a simulated environment, ORT showed improved performance with a 10% increase in success rates and a 30% decrease in failure rates in a 5-goal scenario. Additionally, ORT was shown to effectively reuse previously recalled objects to increase navigation efficiency.

Current approaches to fine-tuning pre-trained language models for specific downstream tasks have several limitations, particularly when applied to low-resource datasets, which often results in overfitting and reduced generalization. To overcome these challenges, our research introduces a novel framework, OPT-IML, that leverages the capabilities of large pre-trained models like GPT-3 to learn task-specific instructions through instruction meta learning. By utilizing the GPT-3 model, OPT-IML enables the generation of task-specific instructions, which are then fine-tuned on the target dataset. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of OPT-IML, yielding state-of-the-art performance on the SNLI, TREC, and STS tasks, with improvements of 1.1%, 1.8%, and 0.4% respectively. Furthermore, our approach outperforms fine-tuning and other meta learning methods, particularly when applied to low-resource datasets, which highlights its potential for tackling low-resource datasets and improving generalization.

Participating in online communities without being a core contributor is known as Lightweight Participation. Although it's a common phenomenon, there's limited research on its impact across multiple online communities. This study examines the role and influence of Lightweight Participants within the Scratch community, a platform for kids to create and share computational ideas, to understand its effects on the community. By analyzing the activities of 101,577 registered users over a 10-year period, the study discovers that 11% of users engage in Lightweight Participation. Further analysis of these users reveals that they primarily contribute by seeking help and contributing small tasks, such as reporting issues. The study finds that these users' actions are crucial for the community's overall activity, particularly in maintaining issue-free code. The study's findings suggest that online communities should implement design strategies to support Lightweight Participation, such as clear guidelines, accessible information, and smaller tasks, to benefit the community as a whole.

A perturbation theory is employed to calculate the thermal properties of the uniform electron gas in the high-density limit using a transcorrelated Hamiltonian with a Jastrow factor. The transcorrelated Hamiltonian simplifies electronic correlations by removing the Coulomb potential between electrons and replacing it with a significantly simpler transcorrelated Hamiltonian. The transcorrelated Hamiltonian's complexity is O(N) while its interaction term is O(N^2). The current research computes the free energy per electron of the transcorrelated electron gas in the high-temperature and high-density limit, which is found to be in good agreement with the random phase approximation and the local density approximation. The transcorrelated electron gas's free energy per electron is calculated to be 0.7799eV for electrons with a density of approximately 0.0124 bohr^-3, which is in agreement with the random phase approximation (0.7836 eV) and the local density approximation (0.927 eV).

In the realm of data assimilation, a crucial aspect is understanding and controlling covariance inflation, particularly in situations where the background error covariance is unknown. We've developed a method to address this by leveraging physical constraints and optimizing the location of observation locations. Our method involves utilizing the available site information to estimate the location of background error covariance, and then utilizing optimal transportation theory to find the most optimal way to spread out the background error covariance. This method is based on the work by Kuo and Ridge in 1992. We've developed a new inflation method that utilizes the trace of the product of background error covariance and analysis covariance. This method is based on the relationship between covariance and observation locations. We've developed a method to estimate the location of background error covariance by solving a nonlinear optimization problem that involves optimal transportation. We've developed a new inflation method that utilizes the location of background error covariance and optimal transportation. Our method is based on the concept of physical constraints and can be used in conjunction with other methods to improve data assimilation performance.

The rapid growth of data in various fields has led to the development of machine learning models that can uncover hidden patterns in data. However, these models often rely on data that is highly interconnected, making it vulnerable to data breaches. To mitigate this risk, we propose an innovative safeguarding method that uses a decentralized approach to break down large data sets into smaller, more secure components and distributes the computation among these components. This method leverages a novel algorithm that randomizes data patterns to further protect the processed information. The safeguarding method is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of machine learning models, and our experiments demonstrate its effectiveness in safeguarding data against privacy breaches.

As robots are increasingly deployed in unstructured environments, ensuring their safety in unfamiliar situations has become a growing concern. We introduce SafeAPT, a novel approach that securely translates learned policies from simulations to real-world robots. This method employs a diverse ensemble of policy models to mitigate potential transfer errors and develops a dynamic risk assessment system that adapts to evolving scenarios. By dynamically updating and refining the risk assessment model, SafeAPT effectively minimizes false positives and remains efficient. Our results demonstrate that SafeAPT significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of both efficiency and safety benchmarks.

The prevailing theory for radio galaxies and blazars is that energy jets emanating from their cores play a pivotal part in their emission. Observations of these jets offer a unique window into their parent black holes and accretion processes. This review aims to summarize the current understanding of jet physics, highlighting areas where further research is required to address the complexities of these high-energy systems. We examine the distinctive characteristics of radio galaxies and blazars, and how they evolve over time. Furthermore, we explore the internal structure and light propagation of jets, and how the properties of radio galaxies and blazars differ in terms of their accretion and black hole characteristics.

This research addresses time-inconsistent models of hidden Markov type within the context of high-dimensional data, focusing on regression analysis. To estimate the model, we introduce a novel approach called sieve time-consistency, which involves approximating the model using a value-itinerary equation that maintains time-invariance. This method enables us to sieve out both the hidden process and time-inconsistent target utility function, using a single error process. Building on this, we create a self-justifying estimator for the target utility function, which is used to derive a set of sieve-based unit root tests for the null hypothesis of time-inconsistency. Furthermore, we propose a sieve-based confidence set for the target utility function, which is shown to maintain size accuracy and achieve asymptotic efficiency. In a simulation study, our method outperforms existing approaches in model parameters and target utility function estimation, and a real-world application of this method is demonstrated through the analysis of a two-factor Chinese inflation model.

The widespread use of social media has led to an increase in the popularity of online platforms, transforming the way people communicate and form relationships. However, the anonymity offered by these online communities enables individuals to express themselves more freely, potentially resulting in the creation of toxic content. This study focuses on tackling the complex issue of identifying offensive language in text, a task that has garnered significant attention within the machine learning community. Our research compares the effectiveness of two neural network approaches, utilizing pre-trained word embeddings and recurrent neural networks, to detect offensive language.

The study of brain connections through functional connectivity holds significant importance.  Traditional FC methods, however, are limited in their ability to account for complex brain dynamics and are heavily reliant on assumptions about the data.  To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel, data-driven approach to FC analysis using deep learning techniques.  This framework, called Data-Driven Functional Connectivity, or D-FC, utilizes a novel neural network architecture that can identify brain connections through complex patterns of neural activity.  Specifically, we use a type of neural network called a generative adversarial network, or GAN, to analyze neural data and identify brain connections.  This approach is tested on simulated data and real-world fMRI scans from the Human Connectome Project dataset, and our results demonstrate the effectiveness of D-FC in uncovering new insights into brain connectivity.  Importantly, we find that D-FC is able to identify brain connections that are not detectable using traditional FC methods, suggesting that it can provide a more complete understanding of brain connectivity.  This research demonstrates the potential of deep learning techniques to advance our understanding of brain connectivity and associated neural disorders.

Building on previous research by Antoshevschi et al., we develop a general framework for applying variational inequalities to nonlinear systems. This approach is demonstrated through a detailed analysis of Nesterov's Nesterov's boosted accelerated gradient method, which is utilized to solve convex optimization problems described by the functional inequality $f(y+\epsilon) - \lambda \sum_{i=1}^m f'(y_i)/r^{k-1} \ge 0$. Our novel framework yields a discrete-time dissipativity theory, which facilitates the derivation of a detailed analysis of NAGA, encompassing both continuous and discrete time stages. The derived analysis is then applied to a range of convex optimization problems, including smooth, non-smooth, and stochastic variants, with the framework's versatility demonstrated.

This research focuses on developing an implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta method for hyperbolic systems with source terms, which is suitable for use at boundaries. By utilizing the penalty approach, we transform the source terms into penalty forces that act on neighboring grid points, enabling the creation of explicit boundary terms. These boundary conditions are then integrated into the Runge-Kutta method, which is designed to be consistent with the implicit-explicit method applied throughout the domain. Additionally, we ensure that the resulting numerical method satisfies the boundary conditions. To achieve this, we introduce a new variable and apply it at a boundary point, maintaining continuity across the boundary and providing high-order accuracy. Furthermore, we conduct a thorough analysis of the proposed method's convergence and stability properties.

Thin and ultrathin silicon layers are commonly used as active layers in photovoltaic and light-emitting devices due to their compactness, however they suffer from reduced absorption due to increased front and back surface reflection. To address this issue, a reflective backing can be employed to significantly decrease the overall absorption loss. Our investigation examines the absorption characteristics of 50 nm and 200 nm thick silicon films, with a 3D photonic band gap reflective backing, utilizing a realistic representation of the silicon material's optical properties. Our results reveal that incorporating this reflective backing can increase absorption in the 200 nm film by 15-22% and in the 50 nm film by 30-45% across a broad wavelength spectrum of 400-1000 nm.

This article presents a novel approach, credval networks, that combines credal sets with valuation networks for decision-making under uncertainty. Credval valuations, a type of lower and upper probability assignment, enable the representation of uncertain quantities and their associated ranges. We outline a framework for credval network learning using the Structural EM algorithm and provide an illustrative case study involving the prediction of diabetes based on patient data.

In the realm of Top-K recommendation, ranking metrics such as AUC and MRR are gaining prominence, and these can be incorporated into a loss function using a metric learning approach. However, the standard metric learning loss often falls short in effectively training the Top-K model, and this issue can be addressed by incorporating a dynamic margin into the loss function. Our research reveals that adaptive margin-based metric learning outperforms traditional methods in various datasets. To take this work further, we've developed a novel probabilistic metric loss framework that automatically adjusts the margin, and experiments demonstrate its superiority over other approaches.

The concept of quantum non-Markovianity has been a focal point in understanding the behavior of open quantum systems. A key development is the classification of quantum channels as either Markovian or non-Markovian based on the dynamics of a specific correlation matrix, known as the quantum dynamical Wigner-Yanase information, or dQWI. Our research reveals that this channel classification is equivalent to distinguishing between the dynamics of the channel's initial and final Kraus operators. Furthermore, we have developed a novel criterion for eternal non-Markovianity that can be applied to any quantum channel. Our results show that any non-thermal quantum channel with a specific type of initial dynamics will exhibit eternal non-Markovian behavior. A notable example of such a channel is the dissipative Pauli X Hamiltonian. Our findings provide new insights into the behavior of open quantum systems and highlight the importance of considering the dynamics of the channel's initial and final maps in distinguishing between Markovian and non-Markovian channels.

The widespread use of AI systems has led to the development of sophisticated machine learning models in various fields, but this has also raised concerns over their potential misuse. A key issue is that these models can be vulnerable to attacks, particularly those that manipulate data to expose their weaknesses. To address this problem and enhance the security of AI-based systems, researchers have proposed a novel counterfactual reasoning framework that combines data analysis with machine learning to identify and mitigate potential risks. The proposed framework consists of three stages: first, it analyzes data to identify potential risks; second, it generates counterfactual explanations to expose vulnerabilities; and third, it evaluates the security of AI models based on the generated explanations. A new algorithm called CFA has been developed to analyze data and identify counterfactual explanations. The proposed framework has been tested using a real-world dataset and achieved promising results in mitigating potential attacks.

The development of semantic maps has been a significant focus area in robotics, with various applications such as robot localization and navigation. To create these maps, robots can either use pre-built environments or build their own, but both methods have limitations. To address this gap, a new simulator has been developed that can generate complex, realistic 3D environments with associated semantic information. This information is captured using the Semantic3D dataset, allowing the simulator to be used to evaluate and compare semantic mapping algorithms across a comprehensive set of scenarios. This research evaluates the performance of three prominent semantic mapping algorithms - ORB-SLAM2, LSTAM, and SLAM-SF, in a variety of challenging conditions, highlighting the simulator's potential to facilitate algorithmic research.

Rikudo is a Japanese sliding tile puzzle played on a 4x4 grid from 15 tiles. It has been proven that finding a winning strategy for Rikudo is computationally hard, belonging to the NP-complete class. As a result, unless a widely accepted assumption is debunked, no efficient method exists to determine if a given Rikudo setup has a viable solution.

Optimal transport techniques have gained significant interest in multiple fields, 
mainly due to their ability to measure distances between data sets. This allows 
the computation of a cost or similarity measure that can be used to compare 
different datasets. By applying optimal transport principles, various machine 
learning tasks can be formulated as computing the closest match between datasets 
and a given reference distribution. This work provides an overview of the current 
state-of-the-art numerical approximations used to solve optimal transport problems, 
and highlights the key considerations for implementing them in machine learning 
applications.

Ramanujan identified a specific type of Ramanujan's congruences for the modular form $c_4$ and extended this to include Hecke groups $\Gamma_k$. This work explores a general theory to explain these congruences using the theory of Goss polynomials from a Drinfeld setting. The congruences can be seen as a result of the polynomial's reduction modulo a prime $p$. A new congruence is also found for a specific polynomial when evaluating it using a field with residue 5.

We have obtained high-resolution R~20,000 and R~40,000 blue-violet spectra of seven lensed quasars through Keck spectroscopy, conducted by L. Cowie and collaborators. These spectra, combined with Hubble Space Telescope images, have allowed us to determine the redshifts of five lensing galaxies and analyze velocity variations within four of these galaxies. Our observations reveal that the lensing galaxies' Tully-Fisher relation aligns with the general trend established by the Cosmic Evolutionary Survey (COSMOS) and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). Furthermore, the observed velocity variations within these galaxies are consistent with the predictions of the cosmological model.

This paper introduces a novel approach for resolving the $q$-fractional differential equation on time scales, and subsequently applies this method to investigate the solutions to the $q$-fractional boundary value problem. Furthermore, we derive distinct characteristic criteria for distinguishing between distinct solutions of the $q$-fractional differential equation and a boundary value problem.

The significance of phonon magnetization in quantum thermodynamics has been gaining attention, particularly its link to a topological feature in the phonon Hall effect. However, a crucial mathematical foundation for this effect is missing, specifically the definition of a phonon magnetic field and phonon magnetic charge. To address this, we develop a topological phonon theory that provides insight into the phonon Hall effect and its relation to topological features. By defining a phonon magnetic field with a specific form and topological currents, we can describe the phonon Hall effect without relying on phonon band structure topology. This effect is revealed to be topologically distinct only when phonon Hall conductivity is considered, ultimately leading to a deeper understanding of the phenomenon.

A highly efficient and versatile Raman imaging method, called Shifted Excitation Raman Difference Spectroscopy with Broad-field (SERDS-BFS), allows for the acquisition of Raman spectra from a large area at high spatial resolution without the need for mechanical scanning. This method, which builds upon the SERDS technology, utilizes the Nod and Shuffle optical system to collect two Raman signals at different wavelengths and compare them. As a result, SERDS-BFS can provide detailed information about the molecular structure of biological samples at various spatial locations. This method has been successfully demonstrated using a CMOS-based microscope that employs the Nod and Shuffle technique, allowing for the acquisition of Raman spectra from a 1mm x 1mm area at a spatial resolution of 10 micrometers. As a proof-of-concept, the SERDS-BFS system has been successfully used to analyze the molecular composition of a single human hair, demonstrating its high spatial resolution and efficiency.
This article presents advancements in research on the Fej\'{e}r and Levin-St\v{c}kin inequalities within the framework of Hilbert-Schmidt operators, as well as exploring related findings.

We investigate the mean null energy condition for an asymptotically flat spacetime 
black hole that's undergoing evaporation. Initially, we demonstrate that a 
spherically symmetric black hole remains stable under this condition, 
meanwhile adhering to the mean null energy inequality. Following this, 
we derive the mean null mean curvature for a Schwarzschild black hole that's 
undergoing evaporation thermally. Subsequently, we derive the mean null 
mean curvature for an uncharged black hole that's experiencing pair creation 
near its axis of symmetry. Ultimately, we discuss the implications of these 
findings in the context of holographic renormalization group flows.

In this lecture series, a set of slides will outline the development and examination of conformal field theories, focusing specifically on the associated operator product expansions and properties of dimensions for primary and secondary operators.

Significant advancements in industrial automation technologies and the Internet have brought about the integration of Industrial Control Systems into the Internet of Things, leading to a convergence of industrial and Information Technology networks. This convergence poses a significant risk of impacting public safety due to potential cyber threats. This paper introduces a cybersecurity testing maturity model for ICS, dubbed ICS-CTM2, which provides a framework for evaluating the effectiveness of existing cybersecurity tests. By assessing actual cybersecurity tests against a comprehensive model of cybersecurity testing, we identified gaps in existing testing methodologies used by vendors. Our research involved analyzing 14 vendor tests and 15 open-source tests against 14 evaluation areas outlined in the ICS-CTM2 model, revealing a lack of standardization and incomplete coverage of cybersecurity testing areas. Our findings indicate that existing testing methodologies fail to address all aspects of cybersecurity, highlighting the need for standardization and improved coverage.

In multi-agent reinforcement learning scenarios, we examine the issue of achieving optimal coordination through value-based methods. These methods are highly effective in single-agent settings but their performance is heavily influenced by the quality of their initial value function. To address this issue, we introduce an approach for estimating an initial value function of high quality using a greedy-based method. This method is efficient as it only requires evaluating actions from the current state. We demonstrate that our proposed approach results in a family of value functions that are close to optimal, thereby allowing existing value-based methods to achieve better performance in multi-agent coordination tasks. Through our analysis, we demonstrate the convergence of our approach to the interval of optimal value functions. Furthermore, we validate the effectiveness of our method using a multi-agent navigation problem and find that it outperforms other approaches.

Pretrained language models have long been shown to exhibit stereotypical biases, 
but recent research has primarily focused on biases present in models trained on 
English language data. This work investigates the prevalence of such biases in 
language models trained on non-English datasets from European countries and 
identifies a previously unexplored bias related to ethnicity. Our study 
demonstrates that language models trained on European data exhibit a strong 
connection between a stereotypical attribute and its corresponding stereotype 
across languages. Specifically, we found that the models often associate female 
speakers with older ages and that this bias is consistent across languages, 
including both English and non-English datasets. Additionally, we found that the 
models' bias is not solely due to the languages used but rather reflects a 
broader societal stereotype. Our results suggest that the models reflect the 
pre-existing biases present in the data used to train them.

Optimizing electrical tilt for solar panels is a complex issue that electrical engineers encounter frequently, which involves adjusting the angle of multiple panels to achieve optimal solar exposure on a building, while adhering to various mechanical constraints. This process can be computationally intensive, necessitating multiple panel adjustments to achieve the ideal orientation. A novel approach to address this challenge is presented, which leverages off-policy reinforcement learning to minimize the number of panel tilt adjustments required to reach the optimal orientation. This approach enables the creation of an optimal tilt policy that can be applied to identical panels to achieve the optimal orientation with minimal adjustments to the tilt angle. The proposed method was tested on a real-world scenario and demonstrated a significant reduction in the number of tilt adjustments needed to achieve the optimal orientation compared to a random policy, while also achieving a faster system adjustment compared to a deterministic policy.

An update is provided for the world's most comprehensive assessment of $C\!P$ violation in the decay of charged $B$ mesons, focusing on the CKM angle $\gamma$. The assessment combines data from LHCb experiments in semileptonic and two-body $B$-meson decays, offering improved precision for a correlated combination. The analysis results in a $\gamma$ angle of $(72.2^{+2.0}_{-1.8})^\circ$ with a confidence level of $1\sigma$. This enhanced determination of $\gamma$ angle surpasses previous records by a significant margin, as well as previous assessments of $C\!P$ violation in $B$-meson decays.

This note delves into the geometric properties of a specific family of ellipsoids, denoted as $\mathcal{E}^n_{A,\theta}$. Each $\mathcal{E}^n_{A,\theta}$ is constructed from a given convex body $A$, by taking the convex hull of points obtained from scaling $A$ and its mirror image across particular hyperplanes. We examine the relationship between real projective transformations and complex symmetries that preserve this family of ellipsoids, ultimately demonstrating a real projection transformation preserves the family if and only if it's equivalent to a complex symmetry.

This paper investigates how the general public perceives personal data markets by examining their opinions and behaviors towards trading and sharing of personal data. A data collection platform was developed to gather information on four types of data and how individuals would engage with them, either by selling, sharing, or disclosing them. The results showed that most participants were hesitant to share their data, prioritizing security over potential benefits. Interestingly, when given a choice, people chose to partly reveal their data instead of keeping it private, which may indicate that individuals are willing to make some information public in exchange for potential benefits, but still aim to maintain control over how it is accessed and shared.

In 5G and beyond, quicker-than-Nyquist (QTN) signaling schemes are gaining traction as a means to increase spectral efficiency. However, detecting QTN signals in the receiver poses a significant challenge due to the increased number of candidate constellations. To address this, this study introduces a neural network-based list sphere decoding (NNLSD) scheme for detecting QTN signals, which involves designing a neural network to predict the number of candidate constellations and another to predict the corresponding modulation symbols. The proposed scheme leverages the characteristics of QTN schemes and integrates the predicted results into the list to achieve significant improvements in detection accuracy and reduced computational complexity. Theoretical analysis confirms that NNLSD achieves a lower decoding time complexity than traditional maximum likelihood (ML) detection for QTN schemes. Experimental results validate the proposed scheme's improved detection performance and reduced computational complexity.

This study explores the order topology and Frink ideal structure within effect algebras. Key findings include the order topology in effect algebras with a total norm having compactness in the Hausdorff topology; the effect algebra having a Frink ideal structure also implies it has a total norm; and in total norm semantics, effect algebras with a Frink ideal structure form a topological space. Additionally, the relationship between the total norm and R0 property in effect algebras is examined, revealing that effect algebras satisfying R0 property also satisfy the total norm.

Recent research has demonstrated that data augmentation can improve neural network
generalization, particularly when the augmented data closely resembles the test data.
However, simply using a random transformation on input data may not be effective
across different datasets. To address this issue, we introduce a novel data augmentation
method, SaliencyMix, which targets specific regions of input data to enhance model
generalization. By incorporating saliency maps to identify important input data areas,
SaliencyMix generates mixed images by combining original input data with a random
transformation applied to the salient regions. Experimental evaluations on CIFAR-10,
CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-21k demonstrate that SaliencyMix outperforms existing data
augmentation methods, including CutMix and MixUp.

Consider the unitary group $\mathrm{U}_\infty$ and fix a compact subgroup $K$. Let $\mathfrak H_K$ represent the full Iwahori--Hecke algebra associated with $\mathrm{U}_\infty/K$. This algebra possesses a maximal commutative subalgebra $\mathfrak H^\mathrm{sc}_K$, which is isomorphic to the algebra of smooth complex functions on $\mathrm{U}_\infty/K$ that are invariant under the action of the Weyl group. We demonstrate that every linear functional on $\mathfrak H^\mathrm{sc}_K$ extending to $\mathfrak H_K$ must be zero. Additionally, we show that the dual of $\mathfrak H^\mathrm{sc}_K$ consists of the traces on $\mathfrak H_K$ that vanish on $\mathfrak H^\mathrm{sc}_K$. Our proof relies on an explicit spectral decomposition of $\mathfrak H_K$ and the use of the Harish-Chandra--Itzykson--Gaudin approximation to the Casimir element.

A new, flexible gravitational theory known as Altered Gravity (ALG) has been developed to investigate potential deviations from General Relativity. ALG can be tested using various methods, including direct observations, which have thus far shown no signs of departure from GR. A different approach to enhance sensitivity involves analyzing large-scale cosmic patterns and structures. Our research focuses on the integration of two methods: one that utilizes large-scale cosmic patterns to detect shear and another based on the intrinsic alignment of galaxy shapes. By combining these methods, we can test different versions of ALG and potentially identify subtle departures from GR. Our findings indicate that the proposed method is sensitive to a specific type of gravitational phenomena and can potentially detect them with a high level of confidence. Additionally, we discuss the potential for future surveys to refine the constraints on ALG using a combination of cosmic patterns and intrinsic galaxy alignments.

The flow properties of fluids are commonly defined by the viscosity that opposes motion. However, fluids with unique characteristics, such as yield stress, can respond differently to deformation. Theoretical studies have focused on simple, rigidly connected particles in a fluid environment, but our research introduces a new concept: a chain of soft, crosslinked particles that responds uniquely to external forces. The internal structure of these chains allows them to behave like solid materials when subjected to constant forces, but can still flow under periodic forces. Our findings have significant implications for our understanding of soft matter and its interaction with biological systems.

The self-assembly of gold nanoparticles into intricate patterns is a key factor in the therapeutic effects of photoactivated, cancer-targeting nanoscale structures composed of nanoparticles. Understanding how light is absorbed by these particles is crucial for developing targeted treatments. However, the exact structure of these particles and how they respond to heat is still not fully understood. To address this, researchers have developed a new approach that combines data analysis with detailed simulations to study the melting of a specific type of gold nanoparticle. By using this approach, they were able to simulate the behaviour of these particles and compare it to experimental results, revealing that the nanoparticles melt in a highly complex manner. Their findings provide valuable insights into the structure and behaviour of these particles and will contribute to the development of more targeted and effective cancer therapies.

This is the initial part of a study that aims to develop a unified approach to fundamental theorems on function splitting and bifurcations. Our research focuses on a broad category of potential operators, encompassing both singular and periodic boundary value problems. The second segment of this investigation will explore concrete applications within specific physical contexts, such as problems related to buckling, elasticity, and fluid dynamics.

The concept of taste is often seen as a complex mixture of distinct flavors, but research suggests that humans can only truly discern three basic tastes: sweet, sour, and bitter. The perceived fifth taste, of sweetness, is actually an illusion created by various other flavors such as those found in milk and certain fruits. A recent study of taste perception in the fruit bat, however, has led to a new understanding of taste. Bats, like humans, can detect sweetness, but a closer look at their taste organs has revealed that fruit bats can detect a unique fourth taste, of a bitter-sweet nature, in addition to the three basic tastes. This discovery suggests that fruit bats can detect a unique combination of bitter and sweet flavors, rather than distinct ones. This new understanding of taste in fruit bats has significant implications for our understanding of taste perception in general, and could lead to a new classification of the basic tastes. A new tetrahedron of taste has been proposed, with bitter-sweet being a unique combination of the two, rather than distinct flavors. This new understanding of taste in fruit bats has also led to a new hypothesis that fruit bats may have evolved to detect a unique combination of bitter and sweet flavors in certain fruits, rather than distinct ones.
We derive new identities for $(h; q)$-Genocchi numbers and polynomials using the beta function.

In the context of clinical trials, researchers often seek to determine the long-term effects of treatments on patient outcomes by analyzing a sequence of measurements. However, due to the limited dataset available, this goal is challenging to achieve. To address this issue, we present a novel reinforcement learning method that simulates and estimates the long-term effects of treatments on patient health outcomes. Our approach is based on a model that represents the patient's health trajectory as a Markov Decision Process, and we use the estimated MDP to predict the long-term effects of treatments through a value function. We have developed a new algorithm, called EMTP, to learn this MDP from data, and it can be integrated with existing methods to estimate long-term effects. Our approach is scalable and can handle large volumes of data, and it is also capable of handling missing data. Furthermore, we have shown that our method is efficient and can be applied to various clinical trials, and its effectiveness has been demonstrated through our experiments using multiple datasets.

When conducting case-control studies to identify risk factors for diseases, researchers often rely on interviews to assess exposure history, but their own expectations about disease outcomes influence their questions, causing them to focus more on cases. This leads to biased data where the likelihood of asking about exposure increases for individuals who are already diagnosed with a disease. This bias affects the association between exposure and disease risk if left unaccounted for. We've developed a method to address this bias through weighted data analysis, which can be done either by using pre-collected data to identify underreporting patterns or by creating and applying a model that estimates these patterns. We've applied this method to a well-known study on how smoking affects tuberculosis, using data from a study where participants were more likely to be asked about smoking if they had the disease. Our analysis revealed that under a non-comparability assumption, smoking increased the risk of tuberculosis by 2.79 times (adjusted odds ratio, 95% CI: 1.82-5.51).

Generative models can be trained to compress data using an autoencoder approach, 
wherein the encoded data is maximally independent. The maximum mutual information 
between the encoded and reconstructed data, $I(q_q, q_{\boldsymbol{\theta}})$, equals 
the amount of information in the data, measured by the mutual information between 
the true and encoded distributions, $I(p_q, q_{\boldsymbol{\theta}})$, and is minimized 
when the data is uncompressible. Training generative models with maximum likelihood 
directly maximizes the $I(p_q, q_{\boldsymbol{\theta}})$, but this results in a suboptimal 
encoding $q$ that does not achieve the maximum mutual information $I(q_q,
q_{\boldsymbol{\theta}})$, especially when using non-invertible layers. In this paper, 
we introduce a method to train invertible autoencoders, which directly maximize 
the mutual information $I(q_q, q_{\boldsymbol{\theta}})$, yielding the most compressive 
encodings possible. The proposed invertible autoencoder achieves state-of-the-art 
results in terms of mutual information and reconstruction loss, while also being 
more efficient than existing methods. Furthermore, it provides a more accurate 
representation of the data, which can be used to compute the maximum data 
compression capacity.

The concept of smart cities has been gaining momentum, and these cities typically produce and manage vast amounts of data, often in the form of complex datasets. However, the sheer volume and complexity of this data pose significant challenges for researchers and experts in the field. To address these issues, this paper presents an innovative, data-centric pattern mining approach that can be used for smart city data analysis. Our approach enables the discovery of meaningful correlations between various city data attributes, and it allows for the effective filtering of relevant information. We have successfully implemented our approach using Apache Flink and tested it on real-world datasets from the city of Leipzig.

This study explores the HDG-P0 method for two-dimensional reaction-diffusion equations and generalized Stokes equations, focusing on developing optimal geometric multigrid preconditioners for matrices derived from HDG formulations using polynomial spaces of degree zero or zero-valued polynomials. The proposed multigrid algorithm leverages the coarse grid correction method with V-cycle technology and accelerates convergence by optimizing parameters such as number of levels, relaxation factors, and other settings. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of the multigrid approach by presenting numerical results for both model problems.

Missing data is a widespread issue in medical studies that affects the reliability of observed associations. In response, we have developed a new Bayesian method for evaluating how likely alternative explanations are for observed correlations in missing data scenarios. This approach measures the relative likelihood of missing data by calculating a Bayesian version of the E-value, which is a well-established metric in causal analysis. To compare our approach with frequentistic and Bayesian methods, we analyzed data from a randomized trial examining the effectiveness of a patient-centered care intervention. Our analysis found that, under Bayesian inference, the likelihood of a false association was relatively low, with an E-value close to 1, indicating that the observed correlation was likely genuine. In contrast, frequentistic methods yielded more conservative results, suggesting that the observed association might be spurious.

In crossover trials where multiple treatment groups are tested, subjects receive multiple treatments throughout the trial. Due to the crossover design, certain treatments are withheld from particular groups of subjects at various points in the trial. As a result, missing data from consecutive treatment periods must be handled in analyses. A novel approach to handling missing data from crossover trials is proposed, focusing on probability-based imputation methods. For multiple probability-based imputation methods, the accuracy of data recovery is evaluated through repeated Monte Carlo simulations. A comparison of imputation methods is made, showing that certain methods yield more accurate results than others. A real-world example is also used to demonstrate the application of probability-based imputation methods in analyses involving crossover trials.

This study introduces the concept of a weak monoidal framework on a category and explores its connections to the related notion of a Stasheff A∞-category. The discussion highlights various examples of weak monoidal frameworks and examines how certain, more stringent, conditions can be applied to the associated stunted simplicial objects they induce. Additionally, we demonstrate that stunted simplicial objects derived from associahedra are particularly well-suited for modeling A∞-preorders due to their inherent, more relaxed, nature.

The growing demand for in-memory computing and in-memory processing is driving the need for innovative solutions to overcome the limitations of traditional DRAM. Our proposal, CODIC, is an adaptable infrastructure that empowers users to create custom in-DRAM functionalities, including in-memory computing and processing, through a software-defined framework. CODIC's hardware architecture is designed to be budget-friendly, with a footprint smaller than 1% of DRAM capacity and a cost lower than 1% of total DRAM system expenditure. CODIC is compatible with existing DRAM technology and can be seamlessly integrated into various DIMM formats. Our prototype, implemented on a 16-lane FPGA connected to eight 4GB DRAM chips, can execute various in-memory applications, including single-node machine learning, graph processing, and in-memory computing, with performance improvements ranging from 2 to 32 times.

This paper presents a comprehensive model for designing virtual networks, utilizing functional programming to optimize management and management-coordinated activities in network evolution. By leveraging the functional approach, we develop a flexible model that facilitates dynamic changes to networks, allowing for the efficient creation of new virtual networks via network abstraction. Furthermore, we provide a detailed, step-by-step process for designing physical and virtual networks, which leverages the capabilities of management information bases to manage and manage-coordinate network resources.

To investigate the feasibility of extending the Toric Code's encoding from qubits to qudits, we examine the costs associated with implementing various logical operations, both in qubit form and in the extended framework. By converting operations originally applicable to qudits into a two-qubit setting, we find that, in terms of the number of required operations, this conversion does not significantly impact performance. Nevertheless, multi-qubit implementations generally prove more efficient for stabilizer operations within the extended code, except for stabilizers in three-body interactions, which incur additional costs following the encoding process.

A task control system is crucial for linking observatories, telescopes, and instruments, enabling seamless execution of complex projects that typically span multiple locations and entities. A key factor in achieving this integration is the adoption of standardised interfaces for task execution and data transfer, such as the Scheduling System Interface (SSI) and Observation Data Product (ODP) Interface, within the context of the Virtual Observatory (VO) framework. We introduce OPUS, an open-source task control system developed by the European Southern Observatory (ESO) and the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy (MPIA), which leverages these standards and showcases their application in real-world scenarios, such as the integration with the ALMA Science Archive and Lab.

This research introduces an innovative approach to teaching undergraduate students the basics of IEEE 802.15.1e Ultra Wide Band (UWB) communication systems in wireless networks through an interactive game-based method. The game requires players to simulate a UWB communication process in their virtual environment and employ this knowledge to defend their own base from attacks by other players. By applying game-driven learning, the study aims to make learning more engaging, efficient, and effective for students than traditional educational techniques. Two experiments were conducted: one with a 3D game and a second one with a 2D game, which revealed that while both formats were enjoyable for students, there was no significant difference in terms of learning efficiency between them.

The relationship between ozone and oxygen levels in planetary atmospheres can be used to infer past and future surface conditions, but the uncertainty in the ozone formation process has led to conflicting predictions regarding its sensitivity to oxygen levels. A new model has been developed to investigate the ozone formation process, which shows that ozone levels are highly dependent on oxygen levels, with low altitudes and low temperatures playing a significant role. The model also found that ozone levels are relatively insensitive to factors such as stratospheric temperature and water vapor levels. A comparison with existing models and observations from Earth and Mars shows that ozone levels are typically underestimated in low oxygen environments, with high-latitude oases on Mars providing a valuable case study for testing the model's predictions. The model also suggests that ozone levels are highly sensitive to factors such as temperature and water vapor levels, with low altitudes and low temperatures playing a significant role. The model's predictions are consistent with observations from Earth and Mars, which suggest that ozone levels are highly dependent on oxygen levels, with low temperatures and low altitudes playing a significant role. The model also found that ozone levels are relatively insensitive to factors such as temperature and water vapor levels.

We investigate the quantum Hofstadter model under nonequilibrium conditions where a two-dimensional lattice is stacked into a three-dimensional honeycomb structure. Under a uniform vertical magnetic field, this system exhibits periodic fluctuations in current across the lattice boundaries. However, when a vertical electric field is introduced, this periodic behavior gives way to a stable, direction-dependent current that persists indefinitely. Notably, this direction-dependent current experiences periodic changes in magnitude due to the discrete electric field, resulting in a Hofstadter-like pattern. Our research reveals that the steady-state surface current is a direct consequence of the unique properties of the Hofstadter model's Floquet bands.

Recent advancements in multilingual neural machine translation have led to significant improvements in translating medical texts. However, domain-specific terminology and the challenges of cross-domain generalization remain major obstacles. To address these issues, our study investigates the effectiveness of fine-tuning multilingual neural machine translation on a large corpus of specialized medical texts. We demonstrate that this approach yields substantial gains in translation quality, particularly when the model is further optimized through back-translation. Additionally, our experiments reveal that incorporating domain-specific knowledge through pre-training enhances performance, particularly when the target corpus is limited.

A system consisting of non-extensive electrons, warm ions, positively charged dust, and a second type of ions is examined for the first time using a nonlinear adiabatic approximation. Two types of waves - solitons and shocks - emerge under specific conditions, particularly when a certain background density ratio is exceeded. Interestingly, the introduction of a second type of ions enhances the stability of both wave types, while increasing electron temperature or the number of positively charged dust grains hinders their formation. However, the presence of a second type of ions is found to strengthen solitons but weaken shocks. This study provides insight into shock waves observed in the Earth's magnetosphere and laboratory plasmas, while suggesting new avenues for experimental investigation of the proposed model.

Recent advances in open-source multilingual language models have led to significant improvements in cross-language information retrieval, but the high computational cost associated with these models has hindered their adoption in commercial search engines. In this study, we introduce an unsupervised, context-driven sentence representation learning approach that leverages dense passage retrieval for multilingual datasets. By integrating a multilingual language model with a contrastive loss function, we demonstrate that our method surpasses baseline models in terms of retrieval performance on datasets spanning up to 45 languages, including low-resource languages. Furthermore, our experiments reveal that the proposed method excels in zero-shot cross-language retrieval tasks, particularly when applied to languages that lack labeled data or specific linguistic groups.

Multimodal learning models have been developed to improve performance in various tasks by incorporating information from multiple modalities, but these models often struggle to accurately represent the relationships between different modalities, especially when the modalities they are trained on have different scales. To address this issue, we introduce a novel method called prototypical modal adjustment, a task-agnostic technique that can be easily applied to any multimodal model to enhance their representation capabilities. PMR involves using prototypical vectors as a common modal, which are calculated based on the mutual information between different modalities, to align the modal representations and adjust the modal weights accordingly. Through thorough experiments on diverse multimodal datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of PMR in significantly enhancing the representation and generalization capabilities of multimodal models across different tasks.

In this scenario, we're examining how quarks and gluons move within a fluid-like environment, taking into account interactions that occur at a particular point in space, known as the MOM plane, rather than across different directions. By developing a set of differential equations that account for these complex interactions, we aim to better understand how these particles interact and evolve over time. The results of our model suggest that particles release a significant portion of their internal energy rapidly as they move through matter, which could potentially lead to the formation of quark-gluon plasma.

This study presents a new approach to spoken command recognition, combining a neural network architecture with a tensor decomposition method to reduce computational complexity. Our experimental evaluation on the CMU Red Caps dataset reveals that the proposed system's unweighted frame accuracy and weighted sequence accuracy reach 93.7% and 92.9%, respectively. Notably, the time-consuming training process was completed in approximately one hour using the NVIDIA T4 GPU, resulting in a 10 times speedup compared to traditional recurrent neural network models.

The two most frequently employed approaches for calculating quantum jump trajectories in open quantum systems are based on the stochastic and path integral formalisms. Despite their effectiveness, there exists a gap in the literature regarding the explicit connections between different master equation representations and quantum jump trajectories. This gap is addressed in this work by providing a comprehensive framework that outlines the conditions under which various forms of the master equation yield equivalent quantum jump trajectories. Furthermore, we establish a novel method for calculating non-Markovian quantum trajectories from a non-rotating frame master equation in terms of a Markovian model with an auxiliary environment, and demonstrate its application through a specific example.

The integration of plasmonic nanoparticles with thin-film solar cells has been found to boost their optical performance, primarily by streamlining light transmission and enhancing the cells' absorption capabilities. In this research, we investigated the influence of aluminum nanoparticles' morphology on absorption improvement in thin-film solar cells. We discovered that incorporating these nanoparticles can increase optical absorption by as much as 70% within the solar spectrum, resulting in a corresponding boost in power conversion efficiency from 6.46% to 6.83%. Our findings also suggest that utilizing these nanoparticles can mitigate the negative effects of inherent material defects and provide an added advantage.

Our investigation focuses on the computational limitations of resolving consistent query (CQ) problems that involve general relations and allow for variables to be undefined. The resolution of such problems is known to be an NP-complete problem, and in general terms it's equivalent in difficulty to the 3SAT problem. The resolution of such problems is typically handled through the use of existential and universal quantifiers in a second-order logic framework, and through the use of an enumeration construct in a first-order logic framework. The use of an enumeration construct typically involves an exponential increase in the complexity of the problem, and in general terms it's not possible to resolve such problems efficiently without this construct. In contrast, our research aims to prove that resolving a certain class of CQ problems without using an enumeration construct is possible and efficient, and we aim to demonstrate that this particular class of CQ problems is equivalent in difficulty to the class of problems that involve a certain logical construct and is known to be solvable without this construct.

Deep learning models have become the norm for various computer vision tasks, but their large size and computational requirements make them impractical for deployment on energy-constrained devices. To address this issue, we have developed an efficient, co-designed algorithmic and hardware system for video identification using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. By applying tensor decomposition techniques, our system minimizes the computational complexity of LSTM networks. The decomposed model exhibits a reduced number of parameters, lower latency, and lower power consumption. Furthermore, we have designed a hardware accelerator that takes advantage of the tensor processing unit architecture to achieve significant performance gains. The results show that our system outperforms other energy-efficient models, delivering a 5.7 times improvement in energy efficiency over the original LSTM model.

The MAVLink protocol, widely used in unmanned aerial systems (UAS) hardware components like sensors, actuators, or ground control systems, lacks security measures despite being a crucial component of many communication stacks. This makes it vulnerable to attacks, which can compromise safety and lead to UAS system failures. This paper presents MAVSec, a novel, secure protocol based on MAVLink, ensuring that a UAS remains operational even in the face of potential attacks. A proposed framework for integrating MAVSec into UAS communication stacks is presented, along with a practical application, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through a case study of a UAS under attack.

The widespread use of the internet and its integration with critical systems for mission-critical operations have raised significant concerns regarding the potential for large-scale disruptions and targeted attacks. In order to assess the vulnerability of systems to such widespread outages, network simulation techniques are employed. However, current network simulation tools often fall short in replicating the complexities of modern networks, leading to inaccuracies in simulation results. In response to this limitation, a new distributed network emulator called Kollaps is introduced. This emulator, which can replicate a network with up to 1,000 nodes, is capable of simulating dynamic network topologies, dynamic packet forwarding, and a range of packet manipulation techniques. Kollaps has been designed to facilitate the development of more realistic network simulations, particularly in scenarios where complex network topologies are involved.

The Newman-Penrose map's image in twistor space is complex analytic, 
but determining its domain of dimension four is a complex problem. 
We identify a problem equivalence to a known twistor space concept, 
and use this equivalence to show that a specific problem is solvable 
for a type of complex curve known as pseudoholomorphic curves.

Researchers have developed a novel method for underground visualisation using muons. This approach employs low-energy cosmic muons that pass through the Earth, allowing for detailed maps of underground objects by tracking the scattering of these muons. A new detector has been designed to achieve a high level of precision in the measurement of muon scattering angles, with simulations indicating its potential for producing high-quality 3D images of underground structures. After two years of data collection, analysis results have been presented and used to refine the simulation model of underground objects, including the Hyper-Kamiokande detector itself. This technology offers a unique tool for monitoring the installation of large underground detectors, as well as locating and visualising objects like power cables and water pipes.

This paper introduces a new formal LL(p) parser parsing algorithm leveraging parsing expressions and introduces a QP parser library for C++ that implements this parser algorithm. The parser algorithm's functionality can be compared with Java's parsing framework, and it enables the creation of parsers with memory and stack limitations similar to David Marcus's LL(p) parser. The QP parser library's functionality can be considered analogous to Java's parsing framework, and it includes pre-built parsing expression operators that support this parser library. An example use case demonstrates a simple QP parser using the parser library's parsing expression operators. Furthermore, the study presents a simple QP parser for C++ using the parser library's parsing expression operators.

We investigate the phenomenon of vacuum radiation, specifically the Cherenkov emission, under conditions of finite temperature within a theoretical framework where Maxwell's electrodynamics is combined with Higgs physics. The emergence of this radiation is attributed to a charged particle's acceleration in a two-dimensional setting, resulting in the emission of low-frequency electromagnetic signals. Notably, these emissions exhibit an unusual temperature dependence.

To gauge the predictive prowess of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) in Natural Language Processing (NLP), we've developed an innovative research framework that leverages real-time language data to assess DNN performance over time. By utilizing this framework, we've tracked the accuracy of DNNs in predicting human behavior on a continuous basis. Our research has focused on two prominent models, SPARSE and BERT, which were evaluated on a diverse range of tasks, encompassing word recognition and prediction, as well as more complex applications such as sentiment analysis and topic identification. Our findings indicate that BERT consistently outperforms SPARSE, particularly when processing contemporary language. Furthermore, our study has revealed that BERT's performance is remarkably resilient, as it can effectively generalize to novel contexts, including topics and timeframes, with minimal decline in performance. These results underscore the significance of our research, which has provided the first-ever comprehensive, real-time language forecast of human behavior using DNNs.

We introduce a novel approach for determining the three-dimensional positioning of an object within a two-dimensional image, referred to as the 'turntable factorization problem'. This challenge is encountered in a variety of situations, including object recognition and image reconstruction. Our method diverges from conventional techniques that rely on pre-known information about the object's three-dimensional positioning, instead using observed instances of an object rotating around a single axis to deduce its three-dimensional positioning. We achieve this by developing a new algorithm that can be trained using either synthetic or real-world data. Our method demonstrates effectiveness by accurately determining the three-dimensional positioning of objects in multiple real-world scenarios, including a comparison with established methods.
